en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Jingying Monastery during the Sui Dynasty.
The myriad differences in the Sage’s teachings essentially consist of only two: namely, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The teaching of the Dharma for śrāvakas is called the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; the teaching of the Dharma for bodhisattvas is called the Bodhisattva Piṭaka. Regarding the śrāvakas...
Within the Pitaka, there are two types of śrāvakas:
first, the śrāvaka-śrāvaka, and second, the pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka. Regarding the śrāvaka-śrāvaka:

such a person originally sought the path of a śrāvaka and constantly delighted in contemplating the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, thereby establishing the nature of a śrāvaka. In their final birth, they encountered a Buddha who taught them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, whereby they attained realization of the Path. Because they originally possessed the nature of a śrāvaka and now again hear the voice [of the Dharma] to attain realization of the Path, they are called a śrāvaka-śrāvaka. As it is said in the Sūtra: "For those who seek to be śrāvakas, one teaches the Four Truths."

Based on this statement, those who are pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas are people who originally sought the path of a pratyekabuddha and constantly delighted in contemplating the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). In their final body, they encountered a Buddha who taught them the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, whereby they attained enlightenment. Because their original nature was that of a pratyekabuddha and they awakened to the path upon hearing the voice [of the Buddha] in their final body, they are called *pratyekabuddha-śrāvakas*. As it is said in the sūtra: "For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination."

According to this treatise, although these two differ, they both seek the Lesser Dharma; since they rely on the same teachings and occupy the same stations, that which is taught for the sake of these two types of persons is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
There are also two types of persons taught within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka:
the gradual and the sudden. Regarding those who enter gradually:

these are individuals who, in the past, practiced the Great Dharma, but in the interim studied the Small [Vehicle], and later returned to enter the Great [Vehicle]. Because they enter the Great from the Small, this is called "gradual. Thus, a sūtra states: "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, I now also cause them to enter into this Dharma. This refers to gradual entry.

Regarding "sudden enlightenment": there are sentient beings who have long cultivated roots of goodness corresponding to the Mahāyāna; now, upon first seeing the Buddha, they are able to enter the Great [Vehicle]. Since this greatness does not arise from the small, it is termed "sudden. Thus, a sutra says: "There may be sentient beings who, throughout successive lifetimes, have constantly received my transformation; as soon as they see my body and hear what I say, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is sudden enlightenment.

Those who enter gradually begin with the small and conclude with the great, whereas those of sudden enlightenment enter directly into the profound; although the gradual and the sudden differ, because they both receive the Great [Vehicle] at that time, what is taught for these two types of persons is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Although the holy teachings are numerous, they do not transcend these two; thus Nāgārjuna said:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the Tripiṭaka at Rājagṛha as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, while Mañjuśrī and Ānanda compiled the Mahāyāna sūtras at the Cakravāḍa Mountains as the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* also states: "The Buddha, for the sake of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas practicing the path leading out of suffering, taught the sūtras.

Those who compiled the scriptures collected them into two piṭakas: those teaching the practices of śrāvakas were classified as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka, and those teaching the practices of bodhisattvas were classified as the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

That treatise further states: "Among the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], only the Vaipulya division constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; the remaining eleven divisions constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
This sūtra also says: "Only the Vaipulya division is upheld by Bodhisattvas; the remaining eleven divisions are upheld by those of the two vehicles."

That which is upheld by Bodhisattvas is the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, while that which is upheld by those of the two vehicles is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; thus we know that the teachings of the Sages do not transcend these two.
These two are also termed the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, or the Half-teaching and the Full-teaching; though their names may differ, their meaning is no different.

This present sutra is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka among the two piṭakas; it is a dharma-gate for the gradual cultivation and nurturing of sentient beings. Therefore, the text below states: "First teach the half-syllables, and afterwards teach the full-syllables."
Having already understood the scope of the teaching,
I shall next explain its title.
What is now called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is the specific title of this distinct section of the scripture.

The names of the sūtras differ and are of many kinds: some are named according to the Dharma they teach, some according to the person [who taught them], some according to the events [they describe], some from analogies, some according to both person and Dharma, some from Dharma and analogy, and some according to both event and Dharma; such examples are not limited to one.
This present sutra is named after its Dharma; "Dharma" here refers to the fruit of the Great Parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, and thus it is mentioned at the outset.
This name is insufficient; according to the Sanskrit original, it is called *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
"Mahā" means "great," a term used to praise its excellence.
There are three types of *nirvāṇa*: those attained by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.
To distinguish it from the former two, the prefix "great" is added; thus it is called "Great. Its essence is actually beyond all relative dependence, yet it is manifested by way of contrast.
There are six meanings of "Great" (*mahā*):
first, it is called "Great" because it is eternal; thus the text below states, "The name 'Great' signifies 'eternal'.

Second, it is called "Great" because it is supreme; as in the world, those who are superior people are called "great men," and thus the text below states, "If this person can abide securely in the True Dharma, they are called the most excellent among men"—it is supreme, therefore it is great, and Nirvana is likewise so.
First, it is called "Great" because it is vast; thus the text below states, "The name 'Great' signifies vastness," for its essence exhausts the Dharma-realm, and thus its nature is called "vast.

Second, it is called "Great" because it is numerous; thus the text below states, "It is like a great treasury containing many rare treasures"; Nirvana is likewise, possessing many kinds of wondrous dharma-treasures, and is therefore called "Great. Third, it is called "Great" because it is high;

thus the text below states, "It is like a great mountain which people cannot climb, hence it is called a 'great mountain'"; Nirvana is likewise, as ordinary beings, those of the Two Vehicles, and even those at the tenth stage cannot reach it, and is therefore called "Great."

It is called "Great" because its depth is profound; just as the ocean is named the "Great Ocean" because its abyss is deep, the text below states: "The 'Great' is called 'inconceivable'; its abyssal depth is difficult to fathom, and thus it is termed 'inconceivable'."
In their general essence, they differ in three broad categories:
first, the greatness of essence (*tài-dà*), which refers to *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*; its essence exhausts the true nature and its significance pervades the *dharmadhātu*.
Second, the greatness of characteristics (*xiàng-dà*), which refers to *upāya-nirvāṇa*; there is no transgression it does not eliminate and no virtue it does not perfect.
Third is "greatness of function," which refers to the wondrous and pervasive application of the Nirvana of Response and Transformation;

its skillful transformations are inexhaustible. Thus, the text below states: "The Great Parinirvāṇa can establish the great purpose. Here, "purpose" (yi) is synonymous with "function" (yong). Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called "Great."
Regarding the term "praveśa" (般), it is translated here as "entry.
There are three meanings of entry:
first, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the cessation of delusion and the return to the True, proceeding from cause toward fruit, is called entry.

Second, distinguishing entry based on transformation: demonstrating that there is a cause for the manifestation of extinction, and manifesting the cessation of body and wisdom to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Third, explaining entry by contrasting the true and the responsive: ceasing transformation and returning to the true.
What is discussed here fully possesses three meanings.
Regarding the term "nirvāṇa," some explain it by saying: "It is neither Sanskrit nor Chinese; it is simply the Buddha’s own language."
If we discuss the Buddha’s words, they are all such; how could it be that only the *Nirvāṇa* is so? Therefore, the text below states:

"Various heterodox doctrines, literary compositions, and incantations are all the Buddha's teachings. Although these are the Buddha's teachings, they do not depart from local dialects; if they were to depart from local dialects, the Buddha would have nothing to say. How then can one claim they are neither Indic nor Chinese?
Others further say: "This is an Indian term that encompasses all myriad virtues; since no single name in this land can translate it, the Sanskrit original is retained, and it is called Nirvāṇa."

The essence of nirvāṇa truly possesses all virtues; however, the single name "nirvāṇa" does not exhaustively encompass all these virtues. If the name "nirvāṇa" were to contain all virtues within it, then when proclaiming those myriad virtues, one should not establish further names according to each virtue. Since one establishes distinct names when wishing to speak of the myriad virtues, it is clear that [the single name] is not comprehensive.

If it is argued that there is no name in this region capable of translating [the term], this is not the case; as stated below in the text, the Tathāgata universally addresses sentient beings according to their kind, saying:
"Today, the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa."
"According to the differences in sound, how could it not be translated?
Now, translating it directly according to its primary characteristic, it is called 'cessation' (nirodha).

Translating it indirectly according to its secondary meanings, there are many different names: sometimes it is called 'non-arising,' sometimes 'non-cessation,' sometimes 'not burning,' sometimes 'not weaving,' sometimes 'quiescence,' sometimes 'unconditioned' (asaṃskṛta), and sometimes 'signless' (animitta); such instances are not limited to these alone."
How can it be known that this cessation is not a total extinction?
For now, let us examine this through four points.

First, by tracing back to the past: the Tathāgata has consistently declared in other sūtras that the point where the causes and effects of birth and death are exhausted is what constitutes nirvāṇa. Today’s nirvāṇa is no different from what was previously named; why then would it suddenly be a total extinction?
Second, based on the final testimony: the Tathāgata now, amidst the *pāri* trees, proclaims with a great voice to all:
"I shall now enter parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings are all filled with grief and distress; they approach the Buddha and entreat him to remain.

If Nirvana were designated as the totality of all virtues, then proclaiming these myriad virtues to people should cause sentient beings to rejoice; why, then, do they weep and approach the Buddha to entreat him to remain?
Judging by this evidence, it is clear that [the term] is not used universally.
Thirdly, according to the established local terminology, when foreigners see someone die and perish, they all say, "So-and-so has entered *nirvāṇa*."
When worldly people die and perish, what virtues could they possibly possess in their entirety?

To take the text as proof, consider how the Buddha later praised Cunda for knowing the Tathāgata, saying that he enters *upāya-nirvāṇa* (expedient nirvana) in common with sentient beings. How could worldly sentient beings ever possess those myriad virtues of nirvana that could be shown to be identical [to the Buddha’s]?
It is because the Tathāgata, together with the world, reaches total extinction that it is designated as "nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, after the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he entered parinirvāṇa during the latter part of the night. The following verse states: "This night the Buddha passes into extinction, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted. From this, it is clearly understood that nirvāṇa is extinction and not cessation [of all existence].

Question: If you say that *nirvāṇa* is called "extinction" (*nirodha*), yet the subsequent passage states, "The extinction of the fires of all fetters is called 'extinction' (*parinirvāṇa*); because it is free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is termed *nirvāṇa*," then the meanings of *nirvāṇa* and "extinction" are different. How then can you say that *nirvāṇa* is called "extinction"?
The commentary states:

"In foreign lands, there are many names for cessation (*nirodha*), such as *nirvāṇa*, *vinaya*, and *merudhara*. Because these names are numerous, different terms are applied according to their respective distinct meanings. Thus, the cessation of discursive thought (*vitarka* and *vicāra*) is called *nirvāṇa*; when the fires of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are extinguished, it is given another designation, which is here translated as 'cessation' (*mie*)."

In this region, the term is translated as "small"; however, *nirvāṇa*, *vinaya*, and *merudha* are all translated equally as "extinction" (*mie*). This is similar to how in foreign lands *bodhi* and *mārga* are both translated as "path."
What is cessation? Cessation has four meanings:
first, cessation as the extinction of phenomena, which extinguishes the causes of birth and death and exhausts the fruits of birth and death.
Second is cessation through virtue (*guṇa-nirodha*): because one abandons cultivation and abides in tranquility, it is called cessation.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s true virtues are free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and are thus also called cessation.

Regarding what is called "being free from characteristics": it is like pure *ghṛta* (clarified butter), whose substance, though existent, lacks characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, or white; likewise, it is like the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings, whose substance, though existent, lacks characteristics such as large, small, long, or short.

Nirvāṇa is also like this: although its essence exists, it possesses no single characteristic and no characteristics whatsoever. As stated in the following passage: "That is to say, it is devoid of the characteristics of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; it is devoid of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as male, female, and so forth; indeed, there is not even a self-characteristic to be grasped."

Regarding the term "separation from nature": within the Great Nirvāṇa, all virtues share a single essence and are collectively integrated; there is not a single virtue that maintains its own distinct nature. Just as when the meaning of "permanence" is proclaimed based upon these virtues, there is no separate, independent nature of permanence to be found apart from the virtues themselves, so it is with all other meanings. Therefore, the text below states: "Furthermore, because they are not distinct, they constitute nirvāṇa."

Third is cessation through response (*pratinirodha-nirodha*): following along with the transformation of the world, one manifests the causes for cessation and displays the extinction of body and wisdom.

Fourth is cessation through principle (*tattva-nirodha*): as stated in the sūtras, "The single Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is the ultimate quiescence of all sentient beings; this is the characteristic of nirvāṇa," and so forth.
There are two aspects to the cessation of principle:
first, the emptiness of characteristics, wherein all dharmas of deluded thought are empty and lack any inherent reality;
second, true emptiness, wherein the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the Tathāgatagarbha are free from both characteristics and intrinsic nature.
Regarding "being free from characteristics," as Aśvaghoṣa said:

"It is not characterized by existence, not characterized by non-existence, not characterized by neither existence nor non-existence, not characterized by neither non-existence nor non-non-existence, not characterized by both existence and non-existence, not characterized by its own nature, not characterized by the nature of another, not characterized by neither its own nature nor the nature of another, and not characterized by both its own nature and the nature of another. Thus, it is entirely inconsistent with all such conceptual discriminations of the deluded mind; it is solely the realm of direct realization."

Regarding what is called "separation from intrinsic nature": these dharmas of the Buddhas share a single identical essence, which they mutually integrate; they are not separate, not detached, not interrupted, and not different. Because they possess this identical essence, there is not a single dharma that maintains its own distinct intrinsic nature.
Although the meanings of cessation (*nirodha*) are manifold, they are essentially comprised of these four.

Among these four cessations, the cessation of principle (*li*) is fundamental: by seeing that appearances are empty, the cessation of prior phenomena is accomplished; by seeing true emptiness, the cessation of prior virtues is accomplished; and based on those virtues, function arises, whereby there is the cessation of the response (*nirmāṇa*).
If one explains them according to their distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the first three cessations are designated as nirvāṇa;
if one discusses them by way of their inclusive characteristics (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa*), all four cessations are so. Question:
This sutra fully elucidates all meanings; why then is it specifically called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*?
It is because *nirvāṇa* is its central theme that it is so designated. Furthermore, as it would be impossible to manifest all meanings exhaustively, it mentions *nirvāṇa* by way of illustration.
That is called "cessation" (*śānti*), which will not be elaborated upon here.
There are three meanings of cessation:
first, to cease the causes and effects of conditioned birth and death and enter into the unconditioned is termed "cessation."

Second, the cessation that accords with reality is called "cessation"; thus the text below states, "If one can sever the activities of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called nirvana.
Third, the cessation that transforms and returns to the truth is called "cessation."
This refers to that which is expressed;

the sutra is that which expresses it. In the foreign [Sanskrit] original language, it is called *sūtra*, which here translates as "thread. Because it can string together all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), just as a thread strings flowers, it is metaphorically described as a "thread."
As for the term "sūtra" (jīng), a thread (*sūtra*) can string together flowers, and warp threads (*sūtra*) can hold the woof; because their functions are similar, it is further called a "sūtra.

If one follows its common etymology, "sūtra" means "constant" (*nitya*); as one teaching among the dharmas, it spans from antiquity through the present, existing eternally, and is thus termed "constant."
Chapter on Life Span (1–2). Regarding the "Chapter on Life Span": according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is called the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*);
according to the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is called the "Chapter on Life Span."
In the establishment of chapters (*varga*) in various sutras, there are generally three principles:
some follow from the extensive, some proceed from the concise, and some are named according to their essential characteristics.

This mention of "life span" is spoken concisely; following the request made by Kāśyapa in verse, the text clarifies that through the causes and conditions of his compassion and non-killing, he attains a long life span. It is based on this that the chapter is designated and named the "Life Span Chapter."
The limit of life is called "longevity" (*āyus*); that which is unbroken in its spiritual wisdom is termed "life.

As for "categories" (*nikāya*), it refers to classification; alternatively, "category" may refer to a genus, wherein various types gather together according to what they clarify—hence the term "genus-category" (*nikāya*).
This sutra consists of a total of thirteen distinct chapters; as this chapter marks its commencement, it is designated as the first.
From beginning to end, the text of this sutra is divided into five sections: first, the Introduction;

second, the section on Opening the Doctrine and Revealing Virtue, starting from "Cunda"; third, the section on Distinguishing the Cultivation and Accomplishment of Virtue, starting from the "Three Announcements"; fourth, the section on Refuting the Erroneous and Promoting the Correct, starting from "If a person can know this, they are called a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa"; and fifth, the section on the Tathāgata’s Parinirvāṇa, Cremation, and Offerings.
This latter portion does not exist in foreign editions.
Since there must be a reason for such a transformation, the introduction is clarified first;
once the introduction has been established, it is appropriate to reveal that which is elucidated therein, and thus the second section follows: Opening the School and Revealing its Virtues.

The "Essential Meaning" (*zong*) refers to the perfect and ultimate wondrous fruit of all Buddhas; since the realization of this fruit arises from causes, the third section next explains the virtues accomplished through cultivation.

Once the True Dharma has been opened, there is a desire to transmit and transform others through what has been clarified so that it remains unceasing; thus, the fourth section next refutes the heterodox to lead toward the orthodox, whereby the subsequent text refutes external paths to clarify the orthodox meaning and refutes the various Māras to clarify the orthodox teaching.

When the work of transformation is complete, the Buddha passes away and returns to quiescence; thus, the fifth section next describes the Tathāgata’s manifestation of extinction, with the great assembly of humans and devas performing the cremation and making offerings.
Question: Many people divide this sutra into three parts; for what reason do you now divide it into five? Answer:
It is explained as follows:

It is indeed reasonable to divide the text into three parts according to the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and other sources; thus, in that sūtra, there is a separate introduction preceding the fifteen chapters, and a separate section for the dissemination (*parivarta*) established following them.
The textual structure of this sutra cannot be treated the same as that [sutra], because its fifth division is not a section for circulation (*pravāraṇā*).
Furthermore, when various commentators compose treatises to explain sutras, they most often do not divide the text into three parts.

Among these five [sections], the first is the skillful means for benefiting through transformation; the middle three are the actual benefit; and the last one is the entry into parinirvāṇa after the work of transformation is complete.
Within the first section, the introduction, there are essentially two parts:
first, the introductory narrative of the occasion (nidāna); second, the introductory narrative of testimony and faith (samyak-pratipatti).
The analysis of these two introductory sections consists briefly of five gates:

first, explaining the meanings of the names and clarifying their intended significance; second, elucidating the distinctions between the names of the two sections and clarifying their respective merits and defects; third, clarifying the scope—whether general or specific—of the names of the two sections; fourth, determining the sequence of the texts of the two sections; and fifth, providing an exegesis according to the text.
Within the first section, the meaning of the title is explained first.

Regarding the term "initiation" (*nidāna*): when the Buddha was about to preach the sutra, he first relied upon a specific time and place, gathered the assembly through his supernormal powers, and initiated what was to be taught; this is called "initiation."
Because it initiates and explains [the teaching], it is called the "Introductory Section on Initiation" (*nidāna*).

Regarding the term "authentication of faith" (*śraddhā-pratyaya*): in the past, Ānanda received the Buddha’s teachings and, wishing to transmit what he had heard to future generations, first addressed sentient beings by saying, "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha. By thus establishing its credibility, it is called the "Authentication of Faith."
Based on these reasons for providing testimony and faith as well as for transmitting the sūtra, it is called the "Testimony and Faith Introduction" (*nidāna*).
Such is the meaning of the name.
Next, to clarify the underlying intent: why are there two parts?
Regarding the statement "because there are two sūtras":
the sūtra is truly only one; how could it ever have been two?
Although the essence of the sūtra is one, it can be divided into two based on the time and the persons involved.
There are two types of sutras: first, those spoken by the Tathāgata himself; second, those transmitted by Ānanda.

The teachings spoken by the Tathāgata benefit those of his own time, whereas those transmitted by Ānanda are for the sake of future generations. To distinguish between these two types of sutras, two introductory sections are established: the *nidāna* (introductory) section is established for the sutras spoken by the Buddha, and the *śraddhā-prasāda* (testimony of faith) section is established for those transmitted by Ānanda.
In the second section, first the distinction between the names of the two introductions is clarified, followed by an analysis of their merits and defects.
There are four ways in which these names differ:
first, naming them according to their essential characteristics, they are called the "Initiation" (Nidāna) and the "Testimony of Faith" (Śraddhādhimukti).

Second, they are named according to the person: the "Tathāgata Preface" and the "Ānanda Preface. Regarding the Preface of Origination, that which was performed by the Tathāgata is called the Tathāgata Preface;

regarding the Preface of Verified Faith, that which was composed by Ānanda is called the Ānanda Preface. Third, they are named according to time: the "Present Preface" and the "Future Preface. The Tathāgata Preface is called the Present Preface, and the Ānanda Preface is called the Future Preface.

Fourth, they are named in relation to the sūtra: the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra" and the "Preface Subsequent to the Sūtra. The Tathāgata Preface is termed the Preface Prior [to the sūtra], and the Ānanda Preface is said to be the Preface Subsequent [to the sūtra].

This is called the "Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha," and it is in relation to this sūtra that the preceding and following sections are distinguished. That *samyak-saṃpratyaya-nidāna* (preface of authentication) has another name: the "Preface to the Bequeathed Teaching. Because the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa and left behind these words as instruction, it is called the "Bequeathed Teaching" (*yìjiào*).
The distinctions of their names are as follows.
Next, the gains and losses are explained.
Among these four pairs, the "testimony" (samyag-adhimukti) and the "initiation" (pravartana) do not deviate from their names and meanings.
Regarding the second pair, there is no fault in Ānanda’s name being placed at the beginning; however, the sequence of the Tathāgata is deficient in meaning.
Why is it deficient?

For example, in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, there are five figures who act as catalysts for its inception: the Buddha as the transforming master, the King, the Queen, Candrā, and Śrīmālā. These five together provide the impetus for the teaching.

In most sutras, the initiation [of the discourse] is rarely performed by the Buddha alone; if one were to insist that initiation must be termed a "Tathāgata-prologue," it would lose the significance of initiation by other persons. Since there is a fault in the Tathāgata-prologue, it must be discarded, and thus the Ānanda-prologue cannot be established as its counterpart either.
In the third pair, there is no discrepancy regarding the present, but it is inconvenient regarding the future.
What is the meaning of this?

If the Tathāgata were to preach the sūtra in the present, the sequence established would be called "present"; since the time Ānanda transmits it is also the present, why would the sequence not be considered present as well?

If the sequence of the Tathāgata is spoken of as being present, then Ānanda’s sequence is consequently termed future; thus, when Ānanda’s transmission is being conveyed, the sequence of the Tathāgata should be termed past.
Although the Buddha has passed away, he is regarded as being in the present at the very moment he speaks;
Ānanda is likewise: although he is not yet in the presence of the Buddha, he is also in the present at the very moment he transmits [the teaching].
Since both are present, how can one be singled out and designated as "future"?
For it is precisely because the future possesses that which has passed and must be discarded that the corresponding present phenomenon cannot be established [as its counterpart].
Regarding the fourth pair: before the sutra, there is no fault; after the sutra, it is incongruous.
If you say it is after the sutra, how can it be called a "preface"?
If you call it a preface, then it cannot be after the sutra.

One should know that these two prefaces are related to two respective sūtras and both precede those sūtras; it is not permissible to judge one as being after the sūtra. This is because if it were after the sūtra, it would be inconvenient to discard it, yet the meaning it addresses would also fail to be established prior to the sūtra.
This is because all such names carry their own limitations; therefore, the current commentator retains only the designations "testimony of faith" (*samyak-pratyaya*) and "initiation" (*nidāna*).

Third, to clarify the universal and specific applications of these names: in a universal sense, both prefaces are termed "testimony of faith," as they are equally designated as "initiations. The intent behind establishing the preface is for all to give rise to faith; thus, they are universally termed "testimony of faith," and since they function identically as initiations, they are equally designated as "initiations."

Now, because two distinct introductory sections are established, the Tathāgata’s introduction is specifically termed the "Initiation" (fāqǐ), while Ānanda’s introduction is specifically designated as the "Certification of Faith" (zhèngxìn). These are both considered the distinct introductions;
they are presented according to their respective contexts to clarify their specific functions. What, then, is the meaning of these designations?

The Lesser Sage Ānanda, fearing that others might disparage or slander [the teaching], composed the preface with the sole intent of engendering faith; therefore, contemporary commentators, looking toward his original intention, designate the Ānanda Preface as the "Certification of Faith" (saddharmapratyayana).

The Tathāgata is a Great Sage whom all people revere and trust; the purpose of establishing this introduction is primarily to inspire and incite others, rather than being solely for the sake of instilling faith. Therefore, the present commentator, looking toward its original intent, explains it as an "exhortation."
Regarding the fourth dhyāna, the text proceeds by first presenting divergent views, secondly examining their merits and defects, and finally revealing the correct interpretation.
What are these divergent views?
According to tradition handed down from the past, it is said that within the "Verses on Faith" (*śraddhā-gāthā*), there are five distinct sections:

First, "Thus"; second, "I heard"; third, "at one time"; fourth, "the dwelling place"; and fifth, "those who heard together. Later commentators added "a Buddha" to these, thus generally explaining six elements; such are the differing explanations.
Regarding the terms "gain" and "loss": the phrase "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) is judged to establish the credibility [of the scripture];
as this statement accords with reason, it is a gain. The phrase "At one time the Buddha... and so forth, which is fixed at the end of the sutra, deviates from reason; as such, it is a loss.
What is the meaning of this?
First, it shall be demonstrated by logical reasoning (*vastu*), and subsequently corroborated by scriptural authority (*vyañjana*).
Regarding the demonstration by reasoning: if the Buddha and others were to exist only after this sutra, then prior to the sutra there would be no Buddha; if so, who would have preached this sutra?
At no time and in no place [could it have been spoken];
upon what, then, could such a teaching rely? Before the sutra existed, there was no assembly;
for whom, then, would it have been intended? Since we rely on these very factors as the impetus for its being spoken, how can one categorically judge it to be a post-sutra composition?
Another person further argues for rescue, saying:
"Although the matter occurred previously, it is brought forward later to serve as corroborating evidence for its credibility; therefore, it is judged to have been spoken later.
If this were so, why would this apply only to the five-phrase and six-phrase [passages]?

Prior to the actual exposition, there could have been only events; all verbal accounts were introduced later. Thus, in this sutra, prior to the shedding of blood, at that time there could have been only events, and the words therein were all introduced by Ānanda at a later time.

However, although the six characteristics and so forth in the subsequent text were also introduced later, they can be determined to have occurred before the sutra—simultaneously with the Buddha and others. Why should this not also be the case here?
Based on this inference and verification, it is certainly not reasonable to conclude that the sūtras were compiled later than the Buddha’s lifetime.

Since the factual evidence is thus established, we shall now provide textual proof. As explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha is said to have taught [this dharma] in the second week at the Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This indicates that by comparing the time, location, and other factors, the excellence [of this teaching] is revealed; because this dharma is supreme, it was taught at the earliest time and in the most excellent place.

When the Buddha was about to preach a sutra, he first relied upon the time and place to manifest the excellence of the Dharma; only then did he begin his discourse, clearly making known the time and place as the preliminary introduction to the sutra.

Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra*’s explanation of the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is likewise the same; it asks: "For what reason is [the teaching] located at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha?"

"This dharma is supreme. Thus, the setting establishes the context for the teaching before the discourse begins, clarifying that it is not subsequent to the sūtra itself; such are the gains and losses [of these two parts]. Next, the correct meaning is revealed:

"Thus have I heard" serves exclusively as a certification of faith (*saddhā-saṃsiddhi*); whereas from "At one time the Buddha" onwards, the meaning encompasses both aspects. Taking the sense of the initial occasion of the teaching, it is judged to be the "Introduction" (*nidāna*); taking Ānanda’s citation of what was received to establish its credibility, it is judged to be the "Certification of Faith. Since the meaning encompasses both, they must not be taken one-sidedly.
Within the fifth section, the phrase "Thus have I heard" is first explained through three gates of analysis:
first, the reason for its existence; second, the clarification of its intended meaning; and third, the interpretation of its specific wording.
Thus have I heard: by what causes and conditions does existence arise?
It is due to the Buddha’s teaching.
For what purpose did the Buddha teach?
It was because Ānanda requested it.
For what reason did he request it?
Because Aniruddha had instructed him.
For what reason did he teach?
It was because he perceived that Ānanda’s mind was distressed.
For what reason was the bhikṣu Ānanda distressed?
Because he had witnessed the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
when the Buddha was about to pass away, he lay between the twin śāla trees with his head toward the north.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing that the Buddha was about to pass away, was filled with grief and distress, unable to restrain himself.
Aniruddha awakened Ānanda, saying:
"You are the Dharma-transmitter; why do you not ask the Buddha about the affairs of future lives?
What benefit is there in grieving in vain?"
Ānanda replied, "My mind is now submerged in an ocean of grief; what do I know of what to ask?
Thereupon, Aniruddha instructed Ānanda to request four matters from the Buddha.
"First, [he asked] after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, what shall the bhikṣus take as their teacher?
Second, upon what shall the bhikṣus rely for their dwelling?
Third, how shall one dwell together with bhikṣus of evil character?"
The fourth question was: "What characters should be placed at the beginning of all sutras?
Upon hearing this, Ānanda’s mind became slightly awakened; he received the instruction and requested the Buddha for an answer. The Buddha replied accordingly:
"O bhikṣus, those who take someone as their teacher should take the Prātimokṣa as their teacher; if I were to remain in the world, it would be no different from this."
The Prātimokṣa is the precept; because it is that which bhikṣus train in, it is called their teacher.
Upon what should all bhikṣus rely for their dwelling? They should rely on the four foundations of mindfulness for their dwelling.

What are the four foundations of mindfulness? They are as follows: a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, observing the body with diligence and single-mindedness, removing worldly greed and sorrow; likewise, he contemplates the body externally, and both internally and externally; and he does the same for feelings, the mind, and phenomena. These are called the bases upon which a bhikṣu dwells.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If one abides in the four foundations of mindfulness, it is called one's own domain, and one is not bound by Māra;
if one abides in the five desires, it is called the domain of others, and one is bound by Māra."

Regarding how one should dwell together with a bhikṣu of evil character: one should treat him with the "brahma-penance" (brahmadanda). If he is disciplined and speaks accordingly, one should explain the sūtras that transcend existence and non-existence; the brahma-penance consists of remaining silent and not conversing with him.
Regarding what characters should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras: one should place "Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a grove," and so forth; these words exist because they derive from the Buddha’s original teaching.
Regarding the expression "so it is" (*evam*), its purpose is to engender faith in sentient beings.
How does it engender faith?

By saying "so it is," Ānanda demonstrates his own confidence in the Buddha’s words; he declares that what the Buddha spoke is indeed so, thereby causing other sentient beings to likewise engender faith.

Regarding the phrase "I have heard": Ānanda is himself an insufficient person; if he were to say that this Dharma was spoken by me, many people would not believe it. However, because he says "I have heard," many people develop faith.
One generates faith in this manner.
What is the meaning of faith, and for what purpose is it generated?
Faith is the initial gateway for entering the Dharma and the foremost guide for embracing the Dharma; indeed, one must first generate faith in order to enter the Buddha-Dharma.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that faith is like a hand: "Just as a person with hands can gather whatever precious jewels they desire upon reaching a treasury of gems, yet would obtain nothing at all if they were without hands."

Faith is likewise so: those who enter the Buddha-dharma possess the hand of faith, by which they may gather at will the jewels of the path and the Dharma; yet if one lacks faith, one gains nothing at all.
Next, I shall explain the text. First, regarding the term "evam" (thus), it will first be established by way of the person who uttered it, and then explained.
How is this established?
Traditionally, it has mostly been explained by reference to Ānanda; because what Ānanda transmitted was exactly as the Buddha spoke, it is called "evam" (thus).
To exclude what is merely similar, it is stated again that "it is.
Upon investigating these words, they are explained from the perspective of the Buddha, not from the perspective of Ānanda. How is this known?

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The term 'thus' (evam) is a word of faith and compliance; those who believe say, 'This matter is thus,' while those who do not believe say, 'This matter is not thus.'"
Ānanda, having manifested his faith and compliance with the Buddha’s words, declared what the Buddha had spoken to be thus.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the *Jentāka-sūtra*, it says: "Ānanda said:
'I have heard this from the Buddha.'"
Thus we know that Ānanda’s naming of what the Buddha taught as "thus" (evam) is indeed correct.
It is merely that the local dialects differ; in the *Jentāka-sūtra*, following the linguistic conventions of this region, it says he heard from the Buddha "thus.
In other sūtras, which mostly follow the foreign (Indian) language style, "thus" is placed first, followed by the manifestation of "I have heard" (evaṃ mayā śrutam).
The definition has been stated briefly; how, then, is it explained?
Regarding the term "thus" (*evam*), there are two interpretations. First, the interpretation in terms of the Dharma:

Ānanda said that because the Tathāgata’s teaching accords with all phenomena, it is called "thus" (*tathatā*). When he speaks of principles, he speaks according to principle; when he speaks of things, he speaks according to things; when he speaks of causes, he speaks according to causes; when he speaks of effects, he speaks according to effects. All such words that accord with the Dharma are consistent with the Way, and are therefore called "thus. Indeed, because that which deviates from the Dharma is termed "not," words that accord with the Dharma can be designated as "is."

Second, the explanation in terms of persons: Ānanda says that what Śākyamuni has now spoken is "as" (tathā) what all past Buddhas have spoken; therefore it is called "as. Because it accords with the principles taught by the Buddhas, it is called "thus" (evam). Indeed, that which deviates from what the Buddhas have taught is "not" (a-), while that which accords with what the Buddhas have taught is termed "is" (evaṃ).
Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): Ānanda spoke these words after having already eaten his meal, addressing future sentient beings; therefore, he said, "Thus have I heard.
Hearing is actually the function of the ear; why, then, is it referred to as "I"?
The distinctions among the various faculties are all instruments of my self; they are designated by the name of their master, and thus it is said, "I have heard.
Since there is no person within the dharmas, how can one speak of "I have heard" by designating a master?
The commentary states:
Although within the Dharma there is no fixed master, it is not that conventional designations do not exist; because they guide and govern sentient beings, one may rightly refer to them as "I.

It is like a military force composed of the four divisions of troops: although there is no fixed master, one can still say, "My army is brave and strong," or "My army has defeated the enemy. This case is exactly the same.
Question: Ānanda is a noble person who has realized the Truth; for what reason does he speak of a "self" in the same manner as ordinary people?
Explanation:
Although Ānanda speaks of a self, he is not like ordinary people.
In what way does he differ?
He explains that there are three kinds of self:

First, the "self" spoken of by the mind of view (*dṛṣṭi-citta*): this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, having not yet eliminated the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), speak of the existence of a self within this mind.

Second, the "self" spoken of by the mind of pride (*māna-citta*): this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who, although they have eliminated the view of self, still possess the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), and thus proclaim the existence of a self within this mind.

Third, the "self" as conventional currency (*loka-pravāda-ātman*): this refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who, having already removed both views and pride, conform to worldly convention and speak of the existence of a self.

Ānanda, at the time of the Dharma-council, he was already established in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); having eliminated views and conceit, he spoke of a "self" only in accordance with worldly convention. Therefore, his case is not the same.
Question: Non-self is superior, whereas the existence of a self is inferior; why not follow the superior view and speak of a self according to the inferior one? Answer:
The Dharma for transforming sentient beings must be like this: if one does not speak of "self," by what means could one distinguish between self and other to enable people to recognize them?
Therefore, up until the Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings, all have spoken of "self" themselves.

From the words "At one time" onwards, although the meaning encompasses both [aspects], because this section contrasts with the preceding portion which is exclusively the *śraddhā-prasāda-anukrama* (the sequence of faith and conviction), it is now explained specifically in terms of its function as the *nidāna* (introduction).

Within this, first, the section concerning the Buddha’s clarity [of wisdom] begins with "Together with the Great... and below; the section concerning the assembly clarified by the Buddha follows, with the time being applicable to both.

Within the former, there are three parts: first, clarifying the time of the transformation; second, clarifying the principal agent of the transformation; and third, clarifying the place of the transformation.
Regarding the term "at one time," it refers to the time of transformation.
In explaining this period, we shall first present divergent views, next examine their errors, and finally reveal the correct meaning.

Regarding the term "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), it has been traditionally transmitted since antiquity that there was no temporal sequence between the Buddha’s speaking and Ānanda’s hearing; rather, this phrase eliminates errors in transmission and establishes the opening formula "Thus have I heard. Therefore, it is called "at one time."
The divergent views are as stated above; how then are their errors refuted?
First, the matter shall be established through inference, and subsequently, it shall be corroborated by scriptural testimony.

Regarding the inference from the facts: Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, and after the Buddha had completed his realization, he preached the sūtras only six or seven days later.

According to the Mahāyāna, the Buddha preached the sūtras after the second seven-day period had passed; at that time, Ānanda was still in his mother’s womb and thus did not participate in the assembly. He only left the household life twenty years later and became an attendant thirty years after the Buddha’s passing. Consequently, many of the sūtras spoken prior to this point were not heard by him directly. Nevertheless, although he did not hear them personally, all the sūtras he compiled state "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*); it can be determined that "at one time" is not a term used to distinguish between different periods of transmission.
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, one cannot claim that Ānanda was a provisional manifestation; on what basis, then, could it be said that speaking and listening occur simultaneously?
By such reasoning and verification, one certainly knows that human speech cannot be relied upon as it stands.
How is it known that Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment?
To establish this point, one must understand the circumstances of Ānanda’s naming.
"Ānandata" is a foreign term; in this [language], it means "Joy."
There are three conditions for joy:
first, past causes and conditions.

When Śākyamuni was practicing as a bodhisattva in the past, he saw the Buddha Śākyamuni of a bygone age; his father’s name was Śuddhodana, his mother’s name was Māyā, and his attendant disciple was named Ānanda. The kingdom and its retinue were no different from those of the present, whereupon he made this vow:
"I vow that in the future, when I attain the Way of the Buddha, it shall be no different from now.
By virtue of this original vow, I have now attained the fruition; therefore, my attendant is again named Ānanda."
Second is the present causal condition:
Ānanda was handsome, and all who saw him rejoiced; therefore, he was named "Joy.
Third is the name established by his parents: for what reason did his parents give him the name "Joy"?
Because it arises at the time of joy.
What is the time of joy?
It is when the Buddha attains the Way.

The Tathāgata was nineteen when he left the city to renounce the world; having renounced it, he practiced meditative concentration for five years and practiced self-starvation for six years. His father, the King, perceived that his son’s body had become extremely frail and weak, and he constantly feared he would not survive.
At a later time, when the Bodhisattva knew that fasting was not the path and accepted the milk-rice offering, desiring to attain perfect enlightenment, Māra thought to himself:
"If the Buddha attains the Way, he will empty my realm; before the Way is completed, I shall destroy his resolve."

He then led eighteen billion officials and attendants, bringing various instruments of torment to intimidate the Bodhisattva. At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi of supreme benevolence, causing Māra’s retinue to fall down in disarray.
Once Māra had been defeated, he thought to himself:
"The Bodhisattva’s power is great; I cannot overcome him. I shall instead afflict his father.
He then went to the palace of King Śuddhodana and proclaimed these words:
"Great King, you should know:
Prince Siddhārtha died last night.

Upon hearing these words, the king fell from his bed like a king of fish scorched by hot sand; after a long while he regained consciousness and thought: "My son, had he remained at home, would have become a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin); how could I have expected him to leave the household life and depart empty-handed, with nothing gained?"

Before long, the deity of the Bodhi tree, having witnessed the fulfillment of the Buddha-way, took celestial flowers and went to the palace of King Śuddhodana to offer congratulations, proclaiming these words:

"The Crown Prince of the Earth attained the Way last night; at the moment the morning star appeared, he subdued the hosts of Māra and achieved the Buddha-way. Therefore, I bring these celestial flowers to celebrate this occasion with you."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with doubt:
"Just now a deva said my son was dead, yet now another deva says my son has attained the Way; which of these should I believe?"
The Bodhisattva said, "My words are to be trusted; that which you saw just now was Māra, and he merely sought to trouble you.
Thereupon, the king thought to himself:
"My son was to remain at home as a Wheel-Turning King, but today he has left the household life to become a Dharma-Wheel King; thus, there is no loss on either side.
Previously I heard he had died, and now suddenly I hear he is alive—this is one source of great joy.
Furthermore, I hear he has attained the Way—this is a second source of great joy."

Before long, King’s younger brother Droṇodana gave birth to Ānanda at night; at dawn, he took the child in his arms and went to the king, saying, “My younger brother has fathered this son during the night.”
The King replied, "My son has attained the Way, and you have given birth to a son; as all causes for celebration converge, I shall name him 'Joy' (Ānanda).
Judging by this evidence, Ānanda was certainly born on the very night he attained the Way; for what reason could his speech and hearing have been simultaneous?
The evidence of this is as follows.
Next, let us provide scriptural proof, such as that spoken in the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra* when Ānanda was compiling the Dharma. First ascending the high seat, he spoke this verse:

"When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, at that time I was not present; thus I heard it passed down by word of mouth: the Buddha traveled to Vārāṇasī and, for the sake of the assembly of five bhikṣus, turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths."

However, that sūtra also begins with the words "at one time," and since its oral transmission likewise states "at one time," it is clear that "one time" does not serve to exclude the possibility of error in the tradition; the refutation of this [objection] is thus complete.

Next, the correct meaning is explained: it is precisely because the Tathāgata taught this at the time for conversion that it is called "the time. Since there are many such times for conversion, one distinguishes it from other times; therefore, it is said to be "one."
How is this known?

As it is stated in the original version of that *Bhūmi-sūtra*: "At that time, the Buddha was among the devas. In its separate transmission, the character "爾" (ěr) has been changed to "一" (yī). Since the phrase "at that time" cannot logically refer to what precedes, by changing "爾" to "一," does it not necessarily belong to what follows?
There are many such examples throughout the various sūtras; for instance, as in the following passage:

"At one time I was in the Śīśumāra Grove; at one time I was in the kingdom of Kāśi; at one time I was in Rājagṛha; at one time I was on the banks of the Gaṅgā"—such instances are not limited to these alone.
Regarding the term "Buddha," it designates the principal teacher of transformation; this is translated as "Awakened" (Jue).
There are two meanings to "Awakening":
first, awakening through discernment, such as a person perceiving a thief.
The second is awakening, which is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*), like a person waking from sleep.

As for "discernment" (*saṃbodha*), it refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); since afflictions and their harmful activities are like thieves, only the Noble Ones perceive them and are not harmed by them; therefore, it is called "enlightenment."

Regarding the term "awakening" (*bodhi*): in contrast to the cognitive obscurations, ignorance is like a state of sleep; when noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*) arises, one awakens with brilliant clarity, just as one wakes from sleep. Therefore, it is called "awakening."
Ignorance is of two kinds:

first, the ignorance that is a fundamental fetter, which delusively obscures the true nature; to counteract and eliminate this, one awakens to the ultimate reality of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, and thus it is called "awakening.

Second, ignorance regarding phenomena, which fails to comprehend conventional truth; to counteract and eliminate this, one awakens to the knowledge of all dharmas categorized into the three groups—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and thus it is called "awakening."

Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Because he has attained equal awakening regarding the collection of that which is beneficial, the collection of that which is not beneficial, and the collection of that which is neither beneficial nor non-beneficial, he is called a Buddha."

That which is meaningful is wholesome; that which is meaningless is unwholesome; and that which is neither meaningful nor meaningless is indeterminate. To know all of this is what is called awakening.
Being able to awaken oneself and further able to awaken others, with the practice of awakening brought to ultimate fulfillment, one is called a Buddha (*buddha*).

"Awakening oneself" distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary people; "awakening others" distinguishes him from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; and "the practice of awakening brought to ultimate fulfillment" highlights his distinction from the Bodhisattvas. For these reasons, this title alone is exclusively applied to the Buddha.
"In the kingdom of Kuśinagara" and so forth refer to the location of the transformation; there are four types of distinct locations:
first, a country; second, a region; third, a river; and fourth, a forest.
Within these places where he wandered and transformed others, the term "being in" (zài) is used to designate them.
The country of Kuśinagara is named after its city; this is translated as "Soft Grass," while in the *Āgama* sūtras it is called "Mow City.

As for the "Land of the Mallas," this refers to a specific location distinguished from the general country; because the borders of the kingdom are vast and extensive, it is further specified separately. Since the sons of the Mallas were born in this place, it is therefore called the "Birthplace of the Mallas."

On the banks of the Āciravatī River, there is a separate area where the terrain is still broad; thus, it is further distinguished here, and in this region, it is translated as the "River of Golden Sand."

Regarding the *śāla* tree, although the river remains wide and long when considered in relation to the specific location of the grove, it is nevertheless pointed out that this place is translated as the "Forest of Solidity" (*Sālaguhāvana*). Because it does not change throughout both winter and summer, it is named the Forest of Solidity.
For what reason are two locations established for this land?
The subsequent text will explain it itself; there must be a specific reason for both the land and the river locations. Since the text does not analyze them here, one should not speak of them rashly.
Some people here use these matters to symbolize the Dharma: they say that Kuśinagara is the city of the ṛṣis; since the ṛṣis possess long lives, it symbolizes the Buddha’s longevity.
The birthplace of the Mallas symbolizes the Buddha’s great power, such that he cannot be crushed or subdued by the four māras.
The River of Golden Sand symbolizes that the River of Nirvana contains the sand of Buddha-nature.
The Forest of Solidity represents the Tathāgata’s true body, which is firm and indestructible.
This may be so, but as it is not stated in the sūtras, it cannot be taken as definitive.
From here on, the second section clarifies the assembly in relation to the Buddha through a threefold analysis:
first, an analysis in relation to the Buddha; second, an analysis in relation to the assembly; and third, an analysis based on the mutual relationship between the Buddha and the assembly.
To understand the characteristics of the transformation, it is necessary to seek clarification from the Buddha;
to understand the distinction between the newly transformed and the previously transformed, it is necessary to seek clarification from the assembly;
and to recognize the textual details, it is necessary for the Buddha and the assembly to deliberate together.
Regarding "approaching the Buddha," the Buddha manifests six signs:
first, emitting sound; second, radiating light; third, shaking the earth; fourth, transforming the forest; fifth, purifying the land; and sixth, withdrawing the light back into his mouth.
Among these six, first the correct meaning is established, and subsequently divergent views are refuted.
What is the correct meaning?
Generally speaking, these six all signify cessation and function as its characteristics.
Within this, there is a further division: the first three [verses] summon the assembly, and the latter three initiate the teaching.
Regarding the first three, they are analyzed through two gates.
The first is the manifestation of the cessation of conceptualization:
The first sign, the sound, causes one to know the time of cessation and the person who has ceased;
the second sign, the light, causes one to know the place of cessation;
the third sign, the shaking of the earth, manifests the certainty of cessation and demonstrates that the cessation is irrevocable.

Second, the differentiation of summoning the assembly: First is the sign of sound, which announces the extinction [of the Buddha] so that all may know; this is done to cause sentient beings to feel longing for the Sage and thus come.

Second is the sign of light, which causes them to know the place of extinction and simultaneously removes their afflictions and obstructions. Previously, upon hearing of the Sage’s extinction, those with the intention to go were entangled by afflictions and obstructions such that they could not move themselves; therefore, he emits rays of compassionate light to remove these afflictions and obstructions. Thus, the subsequent text says: "Among those sentient beings who encounter this light, all karmic stains and afflictions are completely eliminated."
The third earthquake urges them to assemble quickly; thus, the great assembly below perceives the sign and is urged to gather.
Within the subsequent three signs, there is also a twofold analysis.
First, the manifestation of cessation:
The first transformation of the forest changes the permanent dwelling place, manifesting that the Sage must depart;
the second, the Pure Land, shows the destination to which he returns, manifesting that the Sage must proceed there;
the third, the gathering of light, shows that the work of transformation is complete, manifesting that his extinction shall not be deferred.
Second, regarding the exhortation to rouse the minds of the assembly, there are two distinct manifestations: First, the transformation of the forest.

When the assembly of this region gathered and saw that the Sage was still present, they hoped the Buddha would not pass into extinction; their resolve to seek the Dharma remained slack. To exhort them, the Buddha transformed the forest to manifest his passing, thereby increasing their aspiration. Second, the pure land.

When the assembly from other regions gathered and saw that the Buddha was still present, they hoped the Buddha would not pass into extinction; their resolve to seek the Dharma remained slack. To exhort them, the Buddha transformed the land to manifest his passing, thereby increasing their aspiration.

Although he had previously known of the cessation [of his life], he said that this cessation was not yet immediate; his lingering affection remained, and his reception of the Dharma lacked earnestness. Therefore, [the Buddha] again exhorted him with diligence, gathering the light back into his mouth. Having fully manifested the virtues of the Dharma, he now demonstrated the cessation of his life, so as to increase [the disciples'] thirsting aspiration and cause them to receive the Dharma upon hearing it.
The principle of correctness is thus.
Next is the section on "Not Differentiated," which contains three parts.

First, the refutation of multiple characteristics: some establish seven characteristics here; the six types are as previously described, with the addition of one for the "manifested hall," making seven in total when combined with the preceding.

If a hall appears atop a forest, the hall constitutes a distinct characteristic; beneath the hall there is a pond, so the pond should likewise be distinct; within the pond there are flowers, so the flowers should also be distinct. Yet the pond, the flowers, and the hall cannot be separated from one another; since the hall serves to adorn the forest, how can they be considered distinct?

Therefore, in the passage below, after describing the manifestation of the hall, it is stated: "At that time, the śāla grove was adorned in various ways, exceedingly delightful, like the Joyful Garden of Uttarakuru. This makes it clear that they are not distinct.

Second, the refutation of the view that there are few characteristics: some establish only four characteristics here, asserting that the shaking of the earth and the purification of the land are not characteristics of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, there are only four.
Why is it that the shaking of the earth is not a characteristic of *nirvāṇa*?
Because the multitude wept with grief, the earth was made to tremble; this was not manifested by the Buddha, and therefore it is not a sign of extinction.
Why is the Pure Land not a sign of nirvana?
The Pure Land arises from the purity of the minds of the great assembly; it is not manifested by the Buddha.
Furthermore, because it was pure and magnificent, it was not a sign of extinction.

If you say that the shaking of the earth was due to the weeping of the multitude and did not signify the sign of extinction, why did the great assembly, seeing the shaking, cease their sorrow and urge one another to go to the Buddha?
Seeing that the appearance of movement is being urged forward, how can it not be a sign?
If movement were not a sign, for what reason would the great assembly collectively suppress it?

If you say the earth is pure because the minds of the assembly are pure, and that this is not manifested by the Buddha, then it is entirely not a sign of cessation; why then does the subsequent passage state, "By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the ground is all soft," rather than saying it is due to the mind?
If the adornment of the land were not a characteristic of cessation, how could the adornment of the groves of trees constitute such a characteristic?
If they can constitute a characteristic, this case is the same.

Third, refuting the distinction between manifestation and expression: some say that "the first sound-characteristic manifests the time of cessation, but does not manifest other meanings. Since the moment it is raised within the sound is called the time of manifestation, why would the sound expressing that the Buddha is about to enter *nirvāṇa* not be a manifestation?

Others further claim that "the light merely indicates the place of cessation and does not signify any other meaning. If this were so, the text should have stated that sentient beings encounter the light and thereby know the location; it should not have said that when sentient beings encounter the light, their karmic offenses, defilements, and afflictions are all completely eliminated.

People further say: "For what reason does the forest transform to manifest cessation? Because the forest’s white is the sign of death, it manifests cessation. This is a fresh white, not the white of mugwort; therefore, the text below says: "That forest turns white, like a white crane, and is exceedingly lovely."
The Forest of Lovely Trees (Linbai Kainai) asks: What are the signs of death?

Furthermore, people say that "the Pure Land is intended to manifest and explain pure dharmas, not to signify extinction. This is refuted by the same logic as before: if the Forest of Lovely Trees signifies extinction, why would the Pure Land—which resembles it—not do so as well?
This is the first [classification] based on the Buddha.
The second is a separate classification based on the assembly, where the opening and closing [of categories] are not fixed; it may be divided into two, namely the "new" and the "old."
The combination and separation form three parts:
first, the listing of the original assembly; second, the listing of the new assembly; third, from "At that time, Śrīśāla" onwards, the summary of both the new and the old.
The textual divisions are fivefold:
first, an explanation of the original assembly;
second, from "Sound and Light" onwards, an explanation of how the new assembly, upon seeing the signs, increased their grief and urged one another to go to the Buddha.
3. From "At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples" onwards, it clarifies how the former assembly witnessed these signs and their sorrow increased;
4. From "Furthermore, there were eighty hundred thousand" onwards, it clarifies the gathering of the new assembly like clouds;
5. From "Auspiciously" onwards, it provides a summary of the assembled multitude.

If categorized according to the assembly, there are forty-eight groups: the new and old bhikṣus, together with the bhikṣuṇīs, constitute three; from the first *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* up to the tenth *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, inclusive of the preceding thirteen, constitute twenty-four; from "twenty *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*" down to "Vanaśukla" (林白), there are twenty-four, which together with the preceding total thirty-seven assemblies; after Vanaśukla, the Brahma assembly newly gathers, and the bodhisattvas from the ten directions newly arrive, which together with the preceding total forty-eight.

If one divides them according to the gods of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, as well as the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless bodies throughout the four directions, the assemblies are indeed infinite.
The traditional claim of "fifty-four assemblies" is categorically incorrect; this second section distinguishes [the assemblies] by way of their groups.
Within the third section, "The Assembly of the Buddha’s Radiant Convergence," there are twelve parts: first, clarifying the original assembly; second, summoning the new assembly with sound and light;

third, the new assembly beholding the signs and increasing their compassion; fourth, the Tathāgata shaking the earth to urge them to assemble; fifth, clarifying how the various assemblies see the signs of the shaking and gather like clouds at the Buddha’s dwelling; sixth, clarifying the Tathāgata’s transformation of the forest to exhort and encourage them; seventh, again clarifying how the various assemblies behold the signs, increase their compassion, gather like clouds, and present offerings; eighth, summarizing the gathering of the assembly; ninth, transforming the land to make it pure; tenth, through the purity of the land, the assembly universally perceives the ten directions; eleventh, the Tathāgata withdrawing his light; twelfth, the assembly, due to the withdrawal of the light, wailing in grief and shedding blood. Below, the text provides a sequential explanation according to these twelve sections.
Within the first section, the term "at that time" (*tadā*) refers to the time when the assembly gathered; it means when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kuśinagara.

The term "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) refers to the one who has gathered the multitude: because the Buddha is endowed with all virtues and is revered by the world, he is titled the World-Honored One.
The passage beginning with "Together with" (*sārdham*) refers to the assembled assembly; because the [speaker] himself is included among them, it is termed "together with.
"Great bhikṣus" (*mahābhikṣu*) serves to distinguish that specific group.
"Great" (大) is called *mahā* in foreign lands; this term has three translations here:
first, it means "many," as when many people in the world are called a "great assembly" (*mahājana*);
second, it means "superior," as in surpassing other groups.
The three names are "Great," "Vast," and "Fully Endowed with Supreme Virtue.
*Bhikṣu* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated in five ways:

first, "Terrifier of Māra. When one first leaves the household life, it causes Māra to tremble and fear; for the nature of Māra is defiled and base, and fearing that others might surpass him, he gives rise to timidity and dread.
The second is called the Beggar (bhikṣu), for having left the household life, he possesses no stores and sustains himself by begging;
the third is called Pure Livelihood (brahmacarya), for through right begging he remains free from wrong livelihood;
the fourth is called Destroyer of Evil, for by upholding the precepts he is free from transgression.
The fifth is called "pure observance of the precepts," because the precepts are pure due to being free from evil.
Among these five, the first name is designated according to the beginning; the middle two are based on the sequence; and the final two are designated according to the end.
"Eighty billion hundred thousand" enumerates their number.
"Surrounded before and behind" indicates their location; they were positioned before and behind the Buddha, encircling the Tathāgata.

This is the second section below, concerning the summoning by sound and light, with sound preceding light. Since sound is speech, it clearly expresses the act of summoning; therefore, it is presented first.
"On the fifteenth day of the second month" refers to the time when the sound was uttered.

To be on the verge of extinction is called "approaching" (*lin*). When a sound is heard at dawn, it signifies that by the following night the fire shall be extinguished; since its extinction is not far off, it is said to be "approaching.
This explains the extinction of a transformation-body as *nirvāṇa*; furthermore, the cessation of such transformations and the return to the True [Reality] is also termed *nirvāṇa*.
Question: For what reason does he enter nirvana at this time?
The subsequent sutra explains it itself, based on the *Āgama*: "The Tathāgata entered nirvana on the eighth day of the eighth month."

This same characteristic also appears later in this sutra; therefore, the text below states: "Subhadra, having completed the summer retreat, shall come to my dwelling. For this reason, I previously told Māra Pāpīyān:
'After three months have passed, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.'"
As for the statement that it was on the fifteenth day of the second month, this is due to differences in what was seen and heard.

"By the Buddha's supernatural power" clarifies that the person who uttered the sound may also be called the source from which the sound originated; this is the Tathāgata’s power of mastery (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna), and not any other form of supernormal power.
If one asks how many kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) there are and why they are not others, there are four kinds:
the first is the supernormal power of illusion (*māyā-abhijñā*), which transforms external objects.
Second is the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), by which one transports and transforms one's own body and proclaims with a great voice everywhere;
third is the supernormal power of knowledge of dharmas (*dharma-jñāna-abhijñā*), by which one penetrates all phenomena;

fourth is the supernormal power of noble mastery (*ārya-vaśitā-abhijñā*), by which one can give rise to the perception of pleasure within suffering, the perception of suffering within pleasant things, and the perception of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure within phenomena that are both suffering and pleasure, remaining unswayed by changing conditions; this is called noble mastery.
"Now emitting a great sound" is his second *ṛddhi-vidyā* (supernormal power).
The phrase "emitting a great sound" below specifically clarifies the production of sound;
"emitting a great sound" serves as the general heading.
"Voice" refers to vocal sounds, such as those of the Sanskrit or Chinese languages; its essential nature is sound, which will be explained in detail below.
"Great" (mahā-) has three meanings:
first, it is great because it is vast and far-reaching; second, it is great because it proclaims universally; third, it is called great because it expounds matters of great significance.
"The sound pervades everywhere, reaching even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)," refers to its first greatness.

It spreads laterally to all other directions and extends upward to the very limit of the Peak of Existence; because the perception of compassion marks the ultimate end of the three realms of existence, it is called the "Peak of Existence."

The upper limit has already been clarified; the others are omitted for brevity. One should know that wherever one goes throughout the ten directions—from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra)—this applies everywhere, not only to this world-system.
"Announcing universally according to each type" is the second great point.

To speak in Sanskrit among those of the Brahma realm and in Chinese among those of the Han realm is called "sound according to the type. This means that a single sound causes people to have different understandings; it is not that many sounds are produced. Because those with the karmic affinity all awaken simultaneously, it is called "announcing universally."
The section beginning with "Today" constitutes the third major division, which contains two parts:
first, the announcement that the Sage is now entering extinction, intended to cause sentient beings to feel longing for the Sage;
second, the raising of doubts to encourage inquiry, intended to cause sentient beings to assemble for their own benefit.
Furthermore, he proclaims the holy extinction to cause sentient beings to present offerings and entreat him to remain, thereby gathering merit;
he raises doubts and encourages inquiry to cause sentient beings to assemble like clouds to request the Dharma, thereby generating wisdom.
In the previous proclamation regarding cessation, the term "this day" indicates the time of cessation;
the phrase "the Tathāgata," etc., identifies the person who has ceased;
and "about to enter parinirvāṇa" announces the event of his cessation.

Among humans, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses the virtue of self-benefit; because he has come to achieve perfect enlightenment by means of the path of reality as it is, he is called the Tathāgata.
