"Arhat" (Ārhant) is the title for one who is "worthy of offerings. Because they have eternally severed all faults and attained realization in accordance with cessation (*nirodha*), they are called "Worthy" (*Arhat*);
furthermore, because they are worthy of being venerated, they are also called "Worthy."
The "Perfectly Complete Knower" (Samyaksaṃbuddha): because his principle is free from partiality or deviation, it is called "Perfect" (Samyak);
because he exhaustively illuminates that principle, he is termed "Complete Knower" (Saṃbuddha).
His own virtues are immeasurable, yet these three are cited for now.

The section beginning with "compassion" (anukampā) concerns the qualities of benefiting others; first, "compassion" and so forth reveal the characteristics of benefiting others, while "the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One" (mahābuddho bhagavān) cites his title as one who benefits others.
Within the characteristics of benefiting others, "pity" (li) refers to compassionate pity and "sympathy" (min) refers to compassionate sympathy; these two are internal mental states.

"Sheltering" (fu) means to provide shelter so that wholesome dharmas may increase, and "protecting" (hu) means to guard against them so that one may remain free from evil; these two are external manifestations.
"Regarding all sentient beings with equanimity" clarifies the preceding "compassion.
"Regarding them as one would Rāhula" uses a specific case to illustrate the general principle.
"Acting as their refuge" and so forth clarify the preceding "protection."
This is explained according to the method of returning [to the source], using the house and so forth as metaphors.
Among the names for benefiting others, "Greatly Awakened" (*mahābuddha*) is a name for the Buddha.
The term "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*) refers to the title of the World-Honored One; his transformative virtues are immeasurable, and this is merely a brief citation thereof.
“About to enter parinirvāṇa” refers to the matter of his passing; “about to” (*jiāng*) indicates that he is on the verge of entering extinction.

In the subsequent exhortation to inquire, the phrase “All sentient beings who have doubts should ask” demonstrates that he himself has no partiality and desires everyone to inquire together; since asking about one case serves as a standard for all others, it is termed “all.”
Because various dharmas bring about birth, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*);
furthermore, because there is much death and rebirth, they are also named "sentient beings.
Since there are doubts that must be resolved, you may inquire about them all.
The phrase "the final question" indicates that [the Buddha] has certainly entered parinirvāṇa and intends for this to be asked with certainty.
Why is there no communal lamentation here?
Upon first hearing the proclamation of his passing, one has not yet reached a definitive conclusion; thus, the signs of grief and distress are subtle, and for this reason, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, although there is compassion, because its characteristics are identical to those discussed later, it is not treated separately here.

Within the section on "light," the initial part clarifies that the Tathāgata emits light that shines everywhere; from the words "among them" onwards, it clarifies how all sentient beings receive benefit through being touched by this light.
Regarding the beginning: "At that time" refers to the moment when the light was emitted.
The term "World-Honored One" identifies the person who emitted the light.
"In the early morning" further clarifies the specific time.
Because the time was ample, he further pointed out the location:
"From its face-gate" clarifies the place from which the light is emitted.
Since the mouth is the face-gate, why does he emit it from here?
Each and every mark of the Buddha encompasses manifold functions; how could one possibly demand them all?

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata emits light from his face, it is mostly for the purpose of bestowing predictions (vyākaraṇa). By subsequently teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall all become Buddhas, he is universally bestowing predictions upon all beings; it is for this reason that he emits this light.
The following clarifies the emission of light.
"Emitting various kinds of light" serves as a general heading;
"its radiance is of diverse colors" generally reveals its characteristics.
"Blue, yellow, red," and so forth, are distinguished and manifested individually; thus there are six distinct colors.
From "the light pervades" onwards, the extent of the light is explained: it illuminates nearby up to the trichiliocosm, and reaches as far as the trichiliocosms throughout the ten directions.
As stated in the treatises, one thousand sets of four continents combined together are called a small chiliocosm;
one thousand small chiliocosms further combined into one are called a medium chiliocosm;
and one thousand medium chiliocosms further combined into one are called a great trichiliocosm.
This trichiliocosm is called a world-system (*lokadhātu-kṣetra*); because it forms and disintegrates simultaneously, it is treated as a single unit, and now the light pervades it entirely.
People say that this light is distinct from the light previously mentioned; how do we know they are different?
These six and those five are thus known to be not the same.
These illuminate the ten directions, while the latter merely covers the assembly; it is clear that they are distinct.
One might calculate that there should be no difference—how then can this be known?
The subsequent text states that "the light rays emitted return and enter through the mouth," and since there is no further mention of emitting light below this point, we know they are one.
If that is so, why are these six divided into five below?
One interpretation states:
because crystal and agate constitute one category of variegated colors, five [types] are subsequently mentioned.
This is the tradition handed down from foreign lands.
Among the rays of light emitted, five are subsumed and one is set aside to facilitate the penetration of the True Dharma; therefore, five are mentioned below, or it may be understood in this way.
Why, then, is it said here that they "illuminate the ten directions," while below it says they "cover the assembly"?
This is because it follows those sentient beings whom he illuminates.
Since the sentient beings illuminated here have not yet assembled, it is said that his words reach the ten directions;
since the assembly below has all gathered, it is said that his words cover the entire assembly.

If what is encompassed by the "lower" category refers only to a single assembly, why does the lower statement say, "Having necessarily completed what was to be done in the ten directions, this is the sign of final nirvāṇa"?
Since it has already been stated that what was to be done in the ten directions has been accomplished, this [passage] clarifies that it is the same for this [world].

In the subsequent section clarifying how sentient beings receive benefit from the light, the term "six destinies" (*ṣaḍgati*) is used to indicate those who receive the benefit; that is to say, all sentient beings within the six destinies who are illuminated by the aforementioned light all receive benefit.
Humans, devas, asuras, and those in the three evil realms are so called "six destinies" (ṣadgati) because they are the destinations toward which one is driven by causes;
because the paths are distinct and different, they are also called "paths" (mārga).
The sutras sometimes speak of five [destinies], which is due to the process of combining and separating them.
Regarding which of the six destinies asuras are subsumed under, the sutras and treatises differ.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are subsumed under the destiny of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

According to the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, they are subsumed within the realms of ghosts and animals; for instance, that Rāhu, the Asura King, was the son of a lion and was thus classified as an animal.
According to the *Gāthā-sūtra*, these beings are subsumed within the three destinies of devas, pretas, and animals.
The mother of Vemacitra was born from a celestial maiden and is thus designated as a deva; therefore, the sūtra says, "You were originally a deva."
Furthermore, in the sutras they are called "inferior devas," whereas here this division of benefits constitutes the six destinies.
The phrase "those who encounter this light" excludes those who lack the necessary conditions.
"Sin, defilement, and all afflictions are completely eliminated" explicitly clarifies the benefits.

"Sin" refers to the retribution for offenses, which constitutes the obstacle of retribution; "defilement" refers to the obstacle of karma; and "afflictions" refer to the obstacle of affliction. Because one encounters the Buddha’s light, all three obstacles are removed.
Furthermore, the defilement of sin is its evil karma; when this karma and these afflictions encounter the light, they are all extinguished.
From here below, the third section clarifies how the new assembly, upon witnessing these signs, increases their compassion.
"All these sentient beings" refers to those who are objects of compassion.
"Having seen and heard this" indicates the cause for the arising of compassion.
Seeing the light and hearing the sound is what is meant by "having seen and heard."
The following reveals the characteristics of compassion: "Great distress in the mind" refers to the affliction of mental action (*manas-karman*);
"raising the voice and weeping," and so forth, refers to the lamentation of vocal action (*vāk-karman*);
and "raising the hands and striking one's head" refers to the sorrowful affliction of physical action (*kāya-karman*).

The physical manifestations of their distress were diverse: some, overcome by profound grief, could not restrain themselves, raising their hands to strike their heads, beating their breasts, and crying out loudly; others suppressed their inner anguish with difficulty, their bodies trembling and their voices choked with sobs and tears.
Question: For what reason does one beat one's head and strike one's chest?
Someone explains it as follows:
Striking one's head manifests that one has lost the guidance of a leader; beating one's chest demonstrates that one's inner heart is not at ease.
This is not necessarily so; rather, it is merely the manner of worldly grief and resentment.

The world’s various expressions of grief and resentment at parting are manifold: some strike their heads, others beat their breasts; some clap their hands, others slap their cheeks, or perhaps trample the ground. Why must each of these necessarily signify something distinct?
From here below begins the fourth section, "Shaking the Earth to Summon the Assembly.
The phrase "at that time" refers to the moment the earth shook.

What follows clarifies the shaking itself: the great earth, mountains, and seas all trembled. This distinguishes the "Great" from the "Small"; thus, the subsequent text states that when only the ground shakes, it is called an "earthquake," whereas when the mountains, rivers, and the waters of the ocean all shake, it is called a "great earthquake. In this context, the specific causes for the shaking of the earth are omitted.
If one were to state it fully, it should be said: "By the Buddha's supernatural power, the earth shook.
This is the fifth section from below, which clarifies how the great assembly, witnessing the signs of the earthquake, hurried to gather at the Buddha’s dwelling. Within this, there are three parts:

first, clarifying how the various assemblies witnessed the signs of the shaking and urged one another; second, from "At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples" onwards, clarifying how the original assembly beheld the signs and their sorrow increased; third, from "Furthermore, there were eighty hundred thousand" onwards, clarifying the gathering of the new assembly.
The beginning has three parts, which correspond to the three preceding characteristics:

first, the earthquake should correspond to the characteristic of being urged to approach the Buddha; second, from "they grasp one another" onwards, it corresponds to the preceding characteristic of light as they express their lamentation; third, from "they further spoke these words: 'The world is empty'" onwards, it corresponds to the preceding characteristic of sound as they again express their lamentation.
The first part consists of two sections:

first, they mutually restrain one another, each urging restraint and saying, "Do not grieve so greatly; if you do not go to the Buddha, your mere sorrow will be of no benefit. Thus, they restrain one another, hoping to entreat the Sage to remain, and as they have not yet reached a definitive decision, they say, "For now, restrain yourselves and do not grieve so greatly.

Second, from the words "You must go quickly" onwards, they urge one another on together; as the three signs appeared repeatedly and the Sage’s parinirvāṇa was imminent, they had to proceed with haste.

The phrase "prostrating with the head and face" (*śirasā vandate*) and so forth clarifies the purpose of the action: it is to request the Buddha to remain. By prostrating, one honors his body; by placing one's own head—the highest part of one's person—upon the Buddha's feet—the lowest part of his—one uses that which is most supreme to pay homage to that which is most humble, thereby manifesting the utmost sincerity and reverence.
Regarding "exhortation" (*quan*): it refers to requesting the Buddha to remain in the world for one *kalpa* or less.

Some commentators explain that requesting him to remain for one *kalpa* manifests the "full-word" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*), while requesting him to remain for less than a *kalpa* symbolizes the "half-word" (*ardha-akṣara*).
Why must it necessarily be so?

If this great assembly already understood the *pūrṇa-akṣara* (the full syllable) and thereby comprehended that the Buddha is eternal, why would they have troubled to request his remaining in the world?

This was merely the assembly’s own expression of hope, primarily looking forward to one kalpa; should their wish not be fulfilled, they hoped for [his remaining] for another kalpa before his parinirvāṇa.
The third section, "The Response of Light and Signs," contains three parts.
First, "Holding Hands": they mutually offer consolation, for they have both lost their honored teacher; thus, they hold hands.

Second, from "Furthermore, he spoke" onwards, he utters words of lamentation. He says the world is empty because it has lost its honored one; since there is no Buddha at this time, he says the world is void.

From "The merit of sentient beings" onwards, he laments his own loss of benefit: because the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there is no one to teach them what is wholesome, and thus his merit is exhausted;
as there is no one to point out evil and instruct them in its severance, unwholesome karma increases and manifests in the world.
The ten unwholesome actions are the various karmas of non-virtue; because they are established by their own nature and further manifested, they are said to "increase.
Their circulation within the world is termed "transcending the world" [in the sense of pervading it].
This is not for the sake of increasing the supramundane dharmas that transcend faults.
Why, then, do we lament in this way?
Having previously received the Buddha’s light, our defilements and impurities were eliminated; yet if the Sage departs once more, who will be able to extinguish our karmic offenses again?
Therefore, this lamentation was made.
From the words "O virtuous ones" onwards, they urge one another to go quickly, to go quickly.
While thus urging one another, they will surely enter before long; such is the reason for the necessity of speed.
In response to these words, he sighed in lamentation and spoke again:
"Empty is the world! Empty is the world! Alas, that which was most honored has been lost!
Why did he speak thus twice?
People say, "The former emptiness destroys and loses the Tathāgata, while the latter emptiness loses the Dharma.
This should not be so; it is simply that the great assembly’s lamentation is profound, and thus they repeatedly speak of emptiness.
Just as people in the world exclaim, "How joyful! How joyful! when they obtain what accords with their wishes, and "How calamitous!
How calamitous! when they encounter what opposes their wishes—why must one speak repeatedly for there to be a manifest sign?
From the words "We [have been]" onwards, there is lamentation over one's own loss of benefit.
The passage beginning with "From now on we shall have no protection" is a sorrowful exclamation directed toward the compassionate protection previously provided during the period of sound.
From "Once far away" onwards, the text raises doubts and questions regarding the preceding section to express lamentation.
Within the preceding section, the initial phrase "We, from this day forth" clarifies that there is no time for rescue.
Previously there were teachers who lost their protective influence later on; therefore, it is said, "from now on.
"There is no rescue or protection" means there is no escape from evil states: for present evils there is no rescue, and for future evils there is no protection.
"Having no one to revere" means there is no place where one accumulates goodness.
To speak of "poverty" is to manifest the loss of having a refuge, meaning one lacks the wealth of the Dharma.
To speak of being "solitary and exposed" is to reveal the failure of having protection; because there is no one to provide rescue and guardianship, one is solitary and exposed.
Regarding the initial phrase "once [the Buddha] has departed" in the middle of the latter section, it is spoken from the perspective of the beginning.

First, there is the distinction between the distant and the near: the śrāvakas constantly follow the Tathāgata; therefore, following the explanation of the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, they are listed first as those who are "near," as exemplified by the assembly of bhikṣus listed above.
The bodhisattvas are not like this, and thus they are discussed later.
Why do the śrāvakas frequently attend upon the Tathāgata?
There are two reasons for this:

first, the wisdom of the śrāvakas is inferior and they are not yet proficient in the Dharma of the Path; although they have attained the fruits of sainthood, their every movement and deportment must always be guided by the Buddha's teachings. Therefore, from the time of his appearance until his parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata constantly establishes precepts for them.

Second, the assembly of śrāvakas has recently received deliverance from the Buddha; having abandoned the state of ordinary beings and attained sainthood, they bear his profound and heavy grace. Although they have attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), they constantly follow and make offerings to him; therefore, they remain close to the Tathāgata.
For two reasons, the Bodhisattva does not draw near to the Buddha:
first, because his wisdom and understanding are so preeminent that he is profoundly conversant with the Dharma of the Path and does not depend upon the Buddha's teaching;
second, because he manifests transformations according to the needs of sentient beings, he does not draw near to the Buddha.
This is the first distinction based on proximity and distance.

Second is the distinction based on physical appearance: the Śrāvakas maintain dignified deportment and possess a majestic and upright appearance that is universally respected by the world; therefore, they are listed first.

The Bodhisattvas, however, adapt their conduct according to those they transform, and thus their bodies have no fixed standard and their appearance and demeanor are not uniform; therefore, they are listed later.
Third, regarding differentiation by virtue, this may also be termed differentiation according to the teachings.
As Nāgārjuna stated, there are two kinds of teaching:
first, the secret teaching; second, the explicit teaching.
In the Secret Teachings (Guhyamantra), the Bodhisattvas, being venerable in virtue, ought logically to be placed first.

For instance, in the teachings revealed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are shown to have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) just like Buddhas; since people generally hold them in high esteem, it is appropriate for them to be listed at the beginning.

The Bodhisattva follows along with those he transforms, manifesting as one who dwells amidst the various outflows (*āsrava*). If people were to hear that the Bodhisattva is superior to the Arhat, they would mostly be startled and find it strange; therefore, [the Bodhisattva] is listed at the end, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and other texts.
Now, following the order of presentation, the śrāvakas are listed first.
Regarding their enumeration, the assembly of śrāvakas is small and thus appears first;
the bodhisattvas are numerous and therefore appear later.
Although there are four meanings [to this], here it is explained based entirely on the latter three.

Within the assembly of śrāvakas, the bhikṣus are listed first and the bhikṣuṇīs afterwards; the bhikṣus are listed first because they are honored as persons and are fewer in number, while the bhikṣuṇīs are listed later because their physical form is inferior and they are more numerous.
Within the assembly of bhikṣus, there are three distinct sections:
first, listing the assembly and praising their virtues; second, increasing compassion upon beholding certain signs; and third, gathering like clouds at the Buddha’s dwelling.
Regarding the first section, the assembly is first listed; the enumeration and the identification of the assembly are clear and can be understood from the text itself.
The following section praises their virtues, beginning with a general praise, followed by a specific one, and concluding with a summary.
"All are Arhats" is the general praise. *Arhat* is a Sanskrit term;

in this [Chinese] language, it is called "Non-arising" (*wusheng*). Translating according to its meaning, it is also rendered as "Non-attachment" (*wuzhu*): non-arising signifies that retribution has ceased, and non-attachment signifies that causes have been exhausted.

The section following "Attainment of Mind" (心得) is divided into two parts. Within these, the first part first praises his perfection of virtues; the section beginning with "Adding Sandalwood" (加栴檀) praises the purity of his assembly.
Regarding the praise for his perfection of virtues, following the subsequent praise of the bhikṣuṇīs, he initially lacks one quality: that all outflows are already exhausted (āsrava-kṣaya).
Comprehensively addressing what was omitted, the text is divided into eight phrases; although there are eight phrases, the substance consists of only four, namely the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
The first four are the primary praise, while the latter four are a further elucidation.

Regarding "the exhaustion of outflows is attained," it clarifies that "birth is exhausted. According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the exhaustion of birth is precisely the wisdom that abandons the accumulation [of suffering]; therefore, the exhaustion of all outflows is termed "the exhaustion of birth."

"Attaining mastery over the mind" clarifies that the holy life (brahmacarya) is established; according to the *Vibhāṣā*, this refers to the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) within the stage of cultivation. When the practice of the path is perfected and one proceeds according to one's will, it is called "mastery over the mind."

"Having completed what was to be done" refers to the knowledge that what was to be done has been accomplished; according to the *Vibhāṣā*, this is the knowledge of the realization of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), for when the merit of realizing cessation is perfected, it is termed "having completed what was to be done."

"Freedom from affliction" (*vairāgya*) refers to not undergoing further existence; according to the *Vibhāṣā*, this is the knowledge that severs suffering. Here, the term "freedom from affliction" is used to indicate the cause by way of manifesting the result: because one is free from affliction, one does not undergo further existence.
These four meanings are explained in detail later.

"Taming the faculties" (*indriya*) reveals that the initial outflows (*āsrava*) have already been exhausted; from the eye to the mind, that which gives rise to consciousness is called a faculty. Because these faculties are well-tamed, the outflows do not arise; this is like a dragon possessing majesty, revealing the aforementioned mastery.

“Accomplishing wisdom” (*siddha-prajñā*) reveals that what was previously to be done has been completed; this refers to the accomplishment of the wisdom of the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*).
“Attaining one’s own benefit” (*ātma-hita-lābha*) reveals the prior departure from afflictions (*kleśa*); since afflictions harm oneself, being free from afflictions is termed “one’s own benefit.”
"Attaining" (*dai*) means to arrive; it is also called "reaching.
The following passage praises the purity of the assembly, noting that they practice together in unison; thus, it says: "Like a sandalwood forest, surrounded by sandalwood trees."
He is fully prepared to sever all that is associated with the aggregates, like a lion king surrounded by lions.
His cultivated virtues universally perfume others, just like sandalwood;
his severed virtues crush evil, resembling a lion.
The preceding section constitutes the individual eulogies.
The phrase "accomplishment" and those that follow serve as the concluding summary.
The term "immeasurable" and so forth summarizes and praises the virtues mentioned previously.
The phrase "All [beings]" and so forth concludes the praise of those previously mentioned as being born through transformation from the Buddha, naming them the true sons of the Buddha.

Within the second section on increasing compassion upon beholding the signs, there are three parts: first, the manifestation of seeing the light; second, the mutual urging and exhortation; and third, the intensification of sorrowful sobbing.
The passion of his love was so profound that his boiling blood was about to emerge; thus, the blood appeared on his body like *pāṭala* flowers.
The six-fascicle sutra states: "It is like the rising sun shining upon green tree leaves, causing the red veins to all become visible."
From this point downward is the third section, on the gathering at the Buddha’s dwelling. Within it, the purpose of the gathering is first clarified: it is for the benefit of sentient beings.

There are five distinct phrases; the first phrase, "for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings," is the general statement, while the middle three are the specific details.
"Accomplishing the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna": the transformative teaching of the Mahāyāna is characterized by the Mahāyāna's departure from marks;

therefore, it is called the "practice of emptiness. "Revealing the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means": the transformative teaching of the Hīnayāna lacks the provisional dispensations of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it is called "skillful means."
Provisional words that conceal the reality are called the Esoteric Teachings (Guhyaka).
Regarding the phrase "in order not to sever the various modes of teaching": worldly dharmas and transformations, as well as worldly practices, are diverse and unequal; thus they are termed "various."
Furthermore, these three may together constitute the Great Vehicle, accomplishing the supreme practice of emptiness of the Mahāyāna and enabling one to enter its realization.

"Revealing" refers to causing entry into the *āgama* [scriptures] below; it reveals the secret teaching to make known that former teachings were provisional, so that they may be discarded and not followed.
"Uninterrupted preaching of the Dharma" causes one to cultivate the present reality.
What is the meaning of this?

It is because the bhikṣus gathered and approached the Buddha’s dwelling, where the Buddha taught them to practice and study the Mahāyāna path of emptiness; others heard this and entered together with them, thereby bringing others to fulfillment.

Because they approach the Buddha, the Buddha refutes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) in their presence, revealing that his former teachings were expedient means and clarifying that his former [teachings] concealed the ultimate reality; this is called the Tathāgata’s teaching of the secret expedient means.
Because they approach the Buddha, the Buddha teaches them to practice the various deeds of the Mahāyāna; this is called "preaching the Dharma in various ways without interruption."
The single phrase, "to tame those who have been born," serves as a summary.
The preceding five phrases clarify the purpose for the assembly;
the phrase "swiftly arriving at the Buddha's abode" correctly clarifies the gathering itself.
"Prostrating to the Buddha," and so forth; having arrived, they pay their respects.
Within the ranks of the *bhikṣuṇī* assembly, the actual [members] are listed first, followed by the provisional.
Among the actual members, there are three divisions, which are the same as those for the *bhikṣus*.
Within the first section, the assembly is first enumerated; by listing their names and citing their number, the nature of the assembly can be understood.
Below, their virtues are praised.
"All of them are also great Arhats" is a general praise.
The section beginning with "all outflows" (*āsrava*) is a specific eulogy.
Within these specific sections, following the precedent above, the text is slightly incomplete.

In the previous section on the bhikṣus, there was first a eulogy for their perfected virtues, followed by a eulogy for the purity of the assembly; here, however, it is abbreviated, and there is no text eulogizing the assembly.
Regarding the section on praising virtues, following the praise of the bhikṣus, there is one phrase missing at the end: "having attained their own benefit.
Including this missing phrase, the text likewise consists of eight lines; the four points of knowledge praised here are no different from those mentioned above.
Regarding the phrase "the exhaustion of all outflows" (*āsrava-kṣaya*): afflictions flow forth in a continuous stream, much like pus leaking from a sore; therefore, they are called "outflows.
There are three distinct types of outflows:
namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). These shall be explained in detail below.
The three outflows (*āsrava*) are not one; therefore, they are called "all" (*sarva*).
When their cessation is completed by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is termed "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*).
The remainder is as explained previously.
From "Also at dawn" below, [the text describes] how witnessing these signs increased his compassion.
From "Also wishing to benefit" below, [it describes] how they gathered at the Buddha’s dwelling;
the wording is as explained above.

Within the section clarifying the provisional [teachings] among the assembly, the passage "Among the community of nuns, there are further nuns who are all bodhisattvas" sets aside the provisional to reveal the real.
The section beginning with "Dragon among humans" praises their virtues from the perspective of the real.
First, he praises his own virtue.
By calling him a "dragon among men," he manifests the person's nobility.

A dragon is the highest among all animals; these nuns and others are the most excellent among humans. Being similar to a dragon, they are metaphorically called "men" and thus termed "dragons among men."
The phrase "as for the rank" and below clarifies the culmination of that position.
"The rank of the Ten Abodes" distinguishes this from the preceding nine abodes.
"Abiding securely and immovably" distinguishes this from the first abode.
The following is a praise of benefiting others.

"Manifesting as women" refers to the transformation of the body for the sake of others; "constantly cultivating the immeasurables" refers to the transformation of the mind for the sake of others; the meaning of the four immeasurables will be discussed separately below.

"Attaining the power of mastery and being able to manifest as a Buddha" refers to the capacity for transformation; because the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*) is sovereign, one is able to act as a Buddha.
Next, the Bodhisattvas are listed; the text also consists of three parts, identical to those of the bhikṣus.
The introduction consists of four parts:
first, the enumeration of the assembly; second, a brief praise of their virtues; third, the listing of their names; and fourth, an extensive praise of their virtues.
Within the initial enumeration of the assembly, the number is invariably stated at the outset.
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" indicates the specific category of this assembly. "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term;

in this land, it is translated as "sentient beings of the Way. These individuals seek the Way, inwardly harbor the practice of the Way, and become perfected persons through the Way; thus they are called "sentient beings of the Way."
Question: Since those of the two vehicles all seek the Way and possess such practices of the Way, for what reason is the name "Bodhisattva" applied exclusively to them? Answer:
[The explanation follows:]...

The term "worthy and noble" (ārya) has both general and specific applications. Generally, it refers to everyone from the *srotāpanna* up to all Buddhas; in this sense, the name is identical with no distinction, as explained in the following passage.

Specifically, however, each case is distinct. To distinguish them now: since the worthy and noble differ, this bodhisattva is specifically designated as a "sentient being on the path" (*mārga-sattva*).
Why is this so? There are three explanations:

first, distinguishing based on the aspirational mind (*praṇidhicitta*) in expectation of the fruit; only these sentient beings seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), while all others do not. Therefore, they alone are called "beings on the path" (*mārga-sattva*). Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* states: "The superior, resolute vow brings about great enlightenment; the verse calls them 'Bodhisattvas'."

Second, when distinguishing according to the mind of understanding in relation to principle: ordinary beings cling to existence, while those of the Two Vehicles abide in non-existence. Since existence and non-existence both deviate from the Middle, they do not accord with the Middle Way; therefore, they cannot be called "beings on the Path.
Only these Bodhisattvas skillfully relinquish both existence and non-existence and accord with the Middle Way; for this reason, they alone are called "beings on the Path."

Third, regarding the classification by way of practice: there are three gates for entering the Buddha-dharma—first, the teaching; second, the meaning; and third, practice. The teaching is shallow, the meaning is deep, and practice is the most supreme.
The Śrāvaka has dull faculties and is named according to the teaching: "voice" (śabda) refers to the teaching; because they awaken to understanding by consuming the voice, they are called Śrāvakas.

The Pratyekabuddha is superior to him and is designated according to the meaning: "condition" (pratyaya) refers to the meaning; because they awaken to understanding through conditions, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.

The Bodhisattva is the most excellent and is named according to their practice: because they are able to accomplish the path of self-benefit and the benefit of others simultaneously, they are called Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to save only themselves, whereas bodhisattvas are not so; they save both themselves and others—this is called the superiority of the path."
"Because they triumph through the Way, they are called 'beings of the Way' (mārga-sattva).
As for "Mahāsattva," this is translated as "Great.
There are three kinds of greatness, as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*:
First is the greatness of aspiration, which aims for great enlightenment;
second is the greatness of practice, which extensively accumulates the various perfections;
third is the greatness of benefiting sentient beings, through the four means of integration and other forms of benefit.

Below the phrase "Dragon among Men," the second section provides a brief eulogy: first, it praises his own virtues by stating "manifesting his body through skillful means"; second, it praises his virtues for benefiting others.
Third, their names are listed, which can be understood according to their individual distinctions.
From "Their minds all... onwards is the fourth section, the extensive praise.
Within this extensive section, the first part is the specific praise, while from "Accomplishing such... onwards is the general concluding praise.

In the specific praise, he extols their merits across the three periods of time: first the present, then the past, and finally the future; within these three periods, he praises both their virtues of self-benefit and benefit for others.

Regarding the present section, it first extols his own virtues; there are five distinct points, the first four of which concern the embracing of the Dharma, and the last one concerns the protection of the Dharma.
Within the first four, "revering and esteeming the Mahāyāna" constitutes the beginning of his own personal practice.
The "vehicle" (yāna) refers to the functional efficacy of its practice; because practice is able to transport one across, it is called a vehicle.
There are three distinct vehicles, namely: the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Buddha-yāna.
That which all Buddhas ride upon is called "Great" because the first two [vehicles] do not possess this [quality].
"Abiding securely in the Great Vehicle" marks the conclusion of the stage of one's own nature (*svabhāva*);
because one has cultivated it to completion and attained non-retrogression, it is termed "abiding securely."
"Profoundly understanding the Mahāyāna" is the beginning of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
Because one contemplates with clarity that which has not yet been cultivated, it is called "profound understanding.
"Delighting in the Mahāyāna" is the end of superior progress.
Regarding what has been explained above, one desires to practice it.
The preceding section was on the "Compendium of Dharmas.
"Guarding the Mahāyāna" refers to the practice of protecting the Dharma.
Because he does not allow others to slander or destroy [the teaching], it is called "guarding"; this meaning will be explained in detail below in the "Chapter on the Vajra Body.
The above has been a praise of his own virtues.
The following praises his altruism: "He skillfully conforms to the world," meaning he transforms the world through the Dharma.
There are two kinds of worlds:
first, the world of sentient beings; second, the receptacle world.
Now, this "World" (loka) follows sentient beings well.

Why is it called the "World"? "World" (*loka*) means time, and "interval" (*antara*) means the middle; because the sentient beings to be transformed do not transcend time and the middle, it is therefore called the "World."
The section beginning with "Making this vow" explains the transformation through supramundane dharmas; the section beginning with "Having, in the past" praises his past virtues.

First, he praises his self-benefit: "Having already cultivated and maintained pure precepts in the past" refers to the abandonment of unwholesome conduct (*duścarita-virati*), while "skillfully maintaining what should be practiced" refers to the gathering of wholesome conduct (*kuśala-saṃgraha*).

The phrase "liberating those not yet liberated" below praises the virtue of benefiting others; "liberating those not yet liberated" refers to conversion through the teachings of the Hīnayāna, while "succeeding the Three Jewels" and so forth refers to conversion through the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
This is as explained in the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma" (*Mingfa pin*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which describes three aspects:
first, causing sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta so that the Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted;

second, revealing and expounding the profound treasury of the twelvefold scriptures so that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted; [and third, gathering the community of disciples so that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted].
By upholding all the dharmas of dignified conduct, they ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.
In the second part, they praise the great vows to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted;
they analyze and reveal the twelve links of dependent origination to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
By practicing the six points of harmonious respect, they ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.

In its third aspect, they plant the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings, causing the sprouts of perfect enlightenment to grow and ensuring that the Jewel of the Buddha is not interrupted;
they protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, ensuring that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
Skillfully guiding the great assembly with a mind free from anxiety or regret, one ensures that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.
Within these three stages, there is also a gradation; first, regarding the Jewel of the Buddha, its gradation is manifested as follows:
the initial stage is able to cause one to resolve upon Bodhicitta and give rise to the aspiration to seek Buddhahood.
In the second section, praising the great vows means praising the arousal of the vow for practice so that one may cultivate it;
in the third section, planting the seeds of the Buddha in the field of birth means transforming them into the seeds of practice.
Next, we shall clarify the hierarchical gradations of the Dharma Jewel:
the first discourse expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures, which constitutes the Dharma of teaching;
the second discourse reveals dependent origination, which constitutes the Dharma of principle.
Among the three sections, the one that "protects and maintains the Dharma" constitutes its practice of the Dharma.
Below, the stages of the Sangha Jewel are clarified:
the first section, on "receiving and maintaining the dharma of dignified deportment," concerns the skillful means of monastic conduct.
In the second section, practicing the six points of harmony means that one’s conduct is established without discord;
in the third section, skillfully guiding the great assembly means that one’s virtue has matured to encompass others.
The following praises the future: “In a future age, you shall turn the wheel of Dharma,” which refers to the virtue of benefiting others.
Because he will attain Buddhahood in the future, he is able to turn the wheel of Dharma;
"Great Adornment" and so forth refer to the virtues of self-benefit, meaning that he adorns himself by means of the adornment of merit and wisdom.
The preceding section constitutes the individual eulogies, while the following provides the summary.
"Accomplishing such as these" summarizes the aforementioned self-benefit; "equally observing sentient beings" and below summarize the aforementioned benefit for others.
The above constitutes the first section, listing the assembly and extolling their virtues.
The description of the gathering through clouds of increased compassion is explained as before. Question:
Why have the various assemblies above failed to offer clear oblations?
Because those who have left the household life abide in the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma) and possess nothing stored away, they have no offerings to present.

Next, the two groups of lay followers are clarified; because the form of the upāsakas is honorable and their number is small, they are placed at the front, while the upāsikās and others, whose forms are humble and whose numbers are great, are manifested as being behind them.
Within the section on the upāsakas, there are four distinct parts:

first, the enumeration of the assembly and praise of their virtues; second, from "At dawn" onwards, the exposition of their service and offerings to the Buddha; third, from "The World-Honored One knew" onwards, the Tathāgata’s refusal of them; fourth, their failure to achieve their aim and remaining at a distance.
These four sections share many similarities with the preceding [sections]; they should be carefully noted and understood.
Regarding the first section, there are four parts:
first, listing the assembly; second, constantly citing the number [of members]. Previously, one "constant" (gaṅgā) was mentioned; now, two are added.

Question: Those who manifest clear realization (*abhisamaya*) among human beings are not many; why is it that here alone the *upāsakas* have these two constants, while the other assemblies gradually increase?
The explanation says:
Now, as these three thousandfold worlds gather together, there are two Ganges Rivers.
Furthermore, according to the distinctions in karmic retribution, many kinds of people exist within a single location; since they all assemble here, there are two Ganges Rivers.

This is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, being consumed by a great conflagration, gods and humans are constantly filling [the world]," and so forth.
Among the various assemblies below, the number constantly increases; such is the pattern for all of them.

Regarding "the upāsakas," this term distinguishes that specific assembly. Here it is translated as "those who dwell near" (*upāsaka*), meaning they dwell in proximity to the wholesome; they are also called "men of virtuous lodging" (*śubhāvasa*), dwelling with a virtuous mind and thus named "virtuous lodging. Furthermore, they are also called "pure-faith laymen" (*qingxin shi*).

Second, from "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) onwards, there is a brief praise of his virtues: "upholding the five precepts" clarifies his freedom from grave transgressions, while "being fully endowed with dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*) manifests his freedom from minor offenses.
The five precepts are the correct practice for laypeople; therefore, they are praised specifically.
Third, under the heading "Their Names," their individual names are listed.
Fourth, from "Deeply Delighting" onwards, their virtues are extolled in detail.

Within this, the first part praises the practice of guarding against afflictions; from "and also desires" (*api ca icchati*) onwards, it praises the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the guarding against afflictions, there is first a general statement, then a detailed exposition, and finally a summary.
"Deeply delighting in the examination of the various gates of antidotes" is the general heading.
Everything examined below is capable of counteracting faults; therefore, they are called "gates of antidotes.
Regarding the phrase "namely," there are immeasurable specific gates of antidotes, but here six types are briefly cited.

First, "suffering," "pleasure," and so forth constitute the eight gates of cultivation: contemplating the dharmas of birth and death as impermanent, suffering, and so on; and contemplating the dharmas of nirvana as permanent, blissful, pure, and so on.
Second, "real" and "unreal" refers to the gateway of the two truths: the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is real, while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is unreal.

Third, "refuge" and "non-refuge" refers to the gateway of aspiration and aversion: turning toward the Triple Gem is called taking refuge, while turning away from false dharmas is called non-refuge; alternatively, proceeding toward supramundane *nirvāṇa* is called taking refuge, while turning one's back on *saṃsāra* is called non-refuge.
4. "Arising and non-arising" refers to the gate of the conventional and the real: the five aggregates do not arise, yet the conventional person constituted by them is called a sentient being.
5. "Permanent and impermanent," etc., refers to the gate of cause and effect: "permanent" and "impermanent" constitute the gate of the effect;
nirvāṇa is permanent, while saṃsāra is impermanent. "Secure and insecure" refers to the gate of causal practice: wholesome conduct is secure, while unwholesome conduct is insecure.
Furthermore, untainted noble practice is peace, while tainted practice is not peace.

Sixth, categories such as "conditioned" and "unconditioned" constitute the gateway of the Four Noble Truths. Regarding "conditioned" and "unconditioned," these pertain to the Truth of Suffering; that which is conditioned is suffering, and this includes conditioned form-dharmas, mind-dharmas, and dharmas that are neither form nor mind.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not suffering; it arises by way of contrast. Space, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are the unconditioned.
"Cessation" (*prahāṇa*) refers to origination (*samudaya*); that which can be ceased is called "cessation. "Non-cessation" is not origination; it arises by way of contrast.
“Nirvāṇa” is cessation; “non-nirvāṇa” arises as its relative counterpart.
“Supreme” (adhipati) is the path, so called because of its excellence; “non-supreme” arises as its relative counterpart.

From "Constant Joy" (*nitya-sukha*) onwards is the third section, the general conclusion regarding the protection of those of the Hīnayāna. This consists of an initial specific praise followed by a concluding summary.

Within the specific praise, only the merits of the present and future are extolled, while the past is not; because the status of an upāsaka belongs to the stage of proximate practice (*upacara*), it is briefly omitted from praise.
Regarding the praise within the present, both self and others are praised.
The text contains three pairs: the first pair concerns the beginning of practice, the second the middle of practice, and the third the end of practice.

"Also desiring to joyfully hear the unsurpassed Mahāyāna" marks the beginning of self-benefit; in contrast to what preceded it, "acting for others as one has heard" marks the beginning of benefiting others—this constitutes the first pair.
“Upholding pure precepts with yearning for the Mahāyāna” refers to the sequence of self-benefit;

by upholding the precepts one leaves behind transgressions and yearns to extensively cultivate wholesome deeds. “Having already satisfied oneself, one further satisfies the thirsts of others” refers to the sequence of benefiting others; this is the second pair.
The phrase "skillfully able to gather" (*susaṃgraha*) and so forth marks the conclusion of the section on self-benefit.
This section consists of three distinct points: the first two lines clarify the practice of gathering the teachings, which involves gathering unsurpassed wisdom and seeking the great fruit;
the line "delighting in the Mahāyāna" clarifies the training in the great cause.
Furthermore, "appropriating unsurpassed wisdom" refers to seeking the realization of the Dharma; "delighting in the Mahāyāna" refers to seeking the teaching of the Dharma.
The single phrase "protecting" refers to the practice of protecting the Dharma.
"Skillfully following" and below marks the conclusion of benefiting others: skillfully conforming to the world and transforming beings through worldly dharmas.
"Delivering those not yet delivered" and so forth refers to transformation through the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
"Delivering those not yet delivered" means causing them to cross over the fruit of suffering; "liberating those not yet liberated" means causing them to sever the cause of accumulation.
"Succeeding the Three Jewels," and so forth, refers to the transformation through the Mahāyāna Dharma; this is the third pair.

The following section praises how he will in the future turn toward benefiting others; that which consists of the "Great Array" (mahāvyūha) and so forth constitutes his own self-benefit, while the "Great Ornamentation" (mahālaṃkāra) comprises his practice of gathering virtuous deeds, and the profound savoring of pure precepts constitutes his practice of avoiding transgressions.
The preceding section constitutes the specific praise, while the following section provides a general summary.
"Able to accomplish all" and so forth summarizes the aforementioned self-benefit; "toward sentient beings" and so forth summarizes the aforementioned benefit for others.
From here below is the second section, which differentiates the offerings to the Buddha. Since those who live as householders possess offerings they can present, this section is set forth below.
The text is divided into four parts;
the first differentiates the various articles of offering.

2. From "Again, they thought: 'The Tathāgata now accepts my offering'" onwards, [they] practiced mindfulness of the Buddha as he, having accepted it, was about to enter nirvana, their hearts filled with grief and distress;
3. From "Each one bringing" onwards, they held offerings to present to the Buddha;
4. From "Lifting their voices in lamentation" onwards, they sorrowfully entreated the Buddha to accept them.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, material offerings; second, from "Each formed this thought: 'If any sentient beings were in want... onwards, it clarifies the offering of practice.

There were eight kinds of offerings: first, incense from fragrant wood; second, precious banners; third, precious parasols; fourth, various musical instruments; fifth, exquisite flowers held aloft; sixth, diverse perfumes; seventh, provisions for food; and eighth, the adornment of the site.
Within the first section, "also at dawn" defines the time [for gathering wood].
"Desiring to perform the *jāva* (cremation)" defines the purpose for which the wood is used; this is translated here as "burning the corpse."
"Each person takes what they wish" correctly clarifies the selection of the wood.

The sandalwood and so forth constitute the substance of the wood; the light, incense, flowers, and banners are the means of adorning the wood; and the two types of vehicles, carts and horses, are the means for transporting the wood.
The second jeweled banner is further adorned with nets;
the third jeweled canopy is interspersed with floral ornaments.
"Within these flower pedestals there are many black bees"—for what reason are they here?
Bees mostly rely on flowers;
why then are they called "black"?
People say it is to symbolize sentient beings who are shrouded in ignorance.
There may be something intended to be indicated that is not explicitly stated in the text, and thus it cannot be determined arbitrarily.
For what reason do you say this is the sound produced by a bee?
It is because there is something being expressed that this [sound] is cited.
The musical performances, flowers, and incense can be understood through their distinct textual classifications.
Regarding the seventh category, "food," the phrase "preparing food for the Buddha and the Sangha" is the general heading, which is then detailed below.
Incense wood and virtuous water constitute the conditions for the food; bitter, sour, pungent, and so forth are the essential flavors of the food.
Below are three qualities that manifest the excellence of the food.

Regarding the conditions for the formation of food, that which is "formed by the water of eight virtues" consists of these eight qualities: it is pure, odorless, light, cool, soft, delicious, pleasant when drinking, and free from affliction after drinking.

The sense-base of pure color, the sense-base of non-putrid fragrance, and these three sense-bases of tangibles—lightness, coldness, and softness; the sense-base of taste as that which is delicious; and the latter two sense-bases of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*): these eight are the functions of water and the qualities of the water-element; therefore, they are called "meritorious qualities" (*guṇa*).
Within the essence and flavor of food, six flavors are mentioned collectively, and "bitter" and so forth are listed by name.
Below, sweet ghee is described as possessing all eight flavors; why, then, are only six mentioned here?
However, the six and the eight are merely terms for separation and combination; when combined they are called six, and when separated they become eight.
Sweetness is divided into three:
first, that which is not bitter is called sweet, as it is the opposite of the bitter taste.
Second, that which is not sour is called "sweet," as it is the opposite of the taste of sourness;
third, that which is not pungent is called "sweet," as it is the opposite of the taste of pungency.

This is similar to how the two tastes of salty and bland are opposites; while there ought to be distinct names for them in foreign languages, here there is no different designation, and they are both generally referred to as "sweet."
Among the latter three qualities, they are first mentioned and then enumerated.
"Light and supple" refers to the functional efficacy of the food; when consumed, it makes the body light and the limbs supple.
"Pure and clean" means that the substance of the food is refined and pure, free from any further impurities.
Regarding the term "in accordance with the Dharma" (yathādharma), it means utilizing things that accord with the Path, such as [pure food], and not alcohol, meat, and so forth.
Among the eight locations, one arrives first and then adorns them:
first one adorns the ground, next the seat, and finally the tree.
The lay followers (upāsakas), who appeared to have the physical forms of ordinary humans, were asked: "How can you adorn a seat as vast as Mount Sumeru?
Śakra replied:
"Although these beings occupy the status of worldly persons, they are all world-transcending, inconceivable bodhisattvas; therefore, they are able to do so."
Furthermore, this is possible because it is manifested through the Tathāgata’s dharma-gate of samādhi; the following sections are all the same.

What has been explained above constitutes the first part, clarifying material offerings (*āmiṣa-pūjā*); what follows clarifies the offering of practice (*caryā-pūjā*), which is also called the offering of Dharma (*dharma-pūjā*). In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, it is termed the "offering of the path leading to the ultimate destination."
Within this, there are three parts:
first, "He forms this thought: 'If any sentient beings lack [anything]... and so forth, which is the mind that contemplates sentient beings;
second, "When making this gift, he is free from desire and hatred... and so forth, which is the mind that guards against afflictions.

3. From "without any other thoughts" (*ananyacitta*) onwards, it concerns the seeking of the bodhicitta; "without any other thoughts" means not seeking worldly blessings or pleasures, but solely aspiring for bodhi and seeking the fruit of Buddhahood.
"All have already become securely established in the bodhisattva path" indicates the possession of the causes for Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the preceding phrase refers to the aspiration to seek Buddhahood, while "securely established" and so forth refer to the practice of seeking Buddhahood.
The preceding section constitutes the first part, which explains the various articles of offering.

The section beginning with "Furthermore, he forms this thought" is the second part, wherein he reflects that his own existence is subject to extinction, and his mind is filled with sorrow and distress.
The section beginning with "Each bringing their own [offerings]" is the third segment, wherein they bring offerings to serve the Buddha.
The section beginning with "Raising their voices to cry out" is the fourth segment, wherein they mournfully entreat the Buddha to accept them.

At first, he wept aloud; from "they further said to one another" below, he spoke words of lamentation; from "he then raised himself up" below, he formally requested the Buddha to accept [the invitation].
"Raising his entire body" was the request with the body, while "and said" was the request with the mouth.
The preceding second section has explained the offerings made to the Buddha;
from here on, the third section concerns the Tathāgata’s non-acceptance.
The phrase "knowing the proper time" explains the reason for this non-acceptance.
Knowing that now is not the time to receive offerings is what is meant by "knowing the time. What constitutes the time for receiving?
There are two such times: [the time for eating and the time for teaching].
First, regarding the time when he consented to receive [the meal], it was during the "Chapter of Cunda";
second, regarding the time when he actually received it, it was during the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly.

In the former instance, at the time of his consent, the Buddha’s permanence was revealed; in the latter instance, at the time of the actual reception, the permanence of *nirvāṇa* was revealed. Since this is neither of those times, he did not accept [the meal].
The term "silence" clarifies the characteristic of non-acceptance. Why must one remain silent?
The Tathāgata, as a Great Being, embodies the Way and possesses few desires; whether accepting or not accepting, he for the most part remains silent.
How can they be distinguished?
They are made known through manifested signs.
To say "not accepted" is precisely to clarify that which is not accepted.
The meaning of this explanation is fourfold:
first, he did not accept it so that all the assembly might equally have the opportunity to make offerings.
If he had accepted this offering, the rest of the assembly would have lost their resolve; how then could they dare to offer anything further?
Second, [the Buddha] did not accept it in order to cause Cunda to offer a gift that would manifest the Dharma;
had he accepted this offering, how would Cunda have dared to further conceive the intention to make an offering?

Third, he wished to cause the assembly to develop a mind of profound respect toward giving; therefore, he did not accept it at this time, reserving acceptance for later in the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly."
Fourth, at this point, the meaning of the Buddha’s permanence had not yet been revealed to Cunda; fearing that the offerings of the assembly would have no destination, he did not accept them.
Below, after the meaning of permanence has been fully revealed to Cunda, he accepts them equally in the "Chapter on the Questions of the Assembly."
Since he now does not accept this offering, the same principle applies to his refusal of those among the remaining assembly below.
Fourth, he retreats and stands back because his purpose is not yet fulfilled; first he fails to achieve his goal, and subsequently he retreats out of sorrow.
Among these, the first principle is first stated and then illustrated by a simile:
the roots of goodness from making offerings to the Buddha are as dear as a child;
that the Tathāgata does not accept them is called "the loss through illness."
That which is bestowed in vain is called "sending to the tomb";
that which lacks merit to return to its origin is called "returning";
that where the intent to give is not fulfilled is called "regret"—the subsequent combinations may be understood accordingly.
Among the upāsikās, there are likewise four sections:

first, listing the assembly and extolling their virtues; second, describing their service and offerings to the Buddha; third, the Tathāgata’s refusal of them; and fourth, their failure to succeed and remaining at a distance.
The first part consists of four sections:

First, the listing of the assembly. "Three *koṭis*" indicates the number; "various *upāsikās*" identifies the specific group—these are called "women dwelling nearby" (*upāsikā*) or "well-dwelling women," with the meaning being the same as explained previously.
Second, from "receiving and upholding" onwards, there is a brief praise of their virtues, which is also to be understood as above.
Third, their names are listed;
fourth, their virtues are extolled in detail, wherein there is first a specific praise and subsequently a summary praise.
Within the specific praise, there are four parts:
First, "being able to endure and uphold the Dharma" and so forth protects the practice of the Hīnayāna;
second, "reproaching domestic ways" protects against the activity of afflictions (*kleśa*);
third, from "self-observation" onwards, there is the extensive protection against afflictions.
4. From "Deeply delighting" (*gambhīra-ruci*) onwards, there is the extensive protection of the Hīnayāna.
In the first part, being able to fully protect and uphold the True Dharma (*saddharma*) constitutes the practice of protecting the Dharma;
from "For the sake of delivering" (*paritrāṇārtham*) onwards constitutes the practice of gathering in people (*pudgala-saṃgraha*).

In the second section, "reproaching the dharma of one's own household" means reproaching the dharma of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) of one’s own body; the meaning of "reproaching" is as explained below.
In the third section, there are two distinct parts:
first, contemplating faults to engender revulsion; second, from the phrase "by these conditions" onwards, cultivating the remedies to eliminate them.
In the first section, there are three parts: first, one initially contemplates five faults of the body;
second, from "It would be better to [use] a cow... onwards, two matters are used to manifest the loss;
and third, from "Therefore, one should... onwards, a summary that engenders revulsion.
In the initial contemplation of suffering, one first contemplates the suffering of the body.

One views the body as being like a snake; this is its internal suffering. For example, it is like four snakes whose natures and characteristics are mutually antagonistic; the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are likewise so: earth is solid and heavy, wind is mobile and light, water is moist and cold, and fire is parched and hot.
Because they are each mutually antagonistic, the body is like four snakes. That various insects gnaw and devour it constitutes its external suffering.
The varieties of suffering are immeasurable; these two are cited here by way of summary.
Regarding the passage "this body is foul-smelling," one contemplates the impurity of the body. There are five types of impurity:
first, impurity of the seed, which consists of the present semen and blood of the parents as the seed, and the past afflictions and karmic bonds as the seed.

Second is the impurity of the dwelling place: while in the mother’s womb, one’s body is situated between the receptacle for undigested food (āmāśaya) below and the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya) above;
third is the impurity of the self-body: the body is composed of thirty-six substances;
fourth is the impurity of its own characteristics: the nine orifices constantly discharge fluids.

Fifth, it is ultimately impure: once this body has died, it is devoured by worms and becomes excrement; burned by fire, it becomes ash; buried, it becomes earth; in the end, there is no purity whatsoever.
In this present text, three types are briefly enumerated:
bodily stench, bondage by craving, and impurity of the seed.
Because the current parents’ semen and blood serve as the seed, the body is foul-smelling and filthy.
Past craving and afflictions serve as the seeds, which is called the bondage of the prison of greed;

the body is like a dead dog, impure in its very substance, with nine orifices constantly flowing, impure in their own nature—namely, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, and the passages for feces and urine. These are the nine orifices.
Below the section "The body is like a city," one contemplates that the body is without self (*anātman*).
Within this, first one should observe its characteristics by employing the metaphor of a city to clarify the body's falsity and insubstantiality; the meaning of the text is clear.
The passage beginning with "Thus this city of the body is abandoned by all Buddhas" uses the person to manifest the Dharma.
That the Buddhas abandon it demonstrates that there is truly no self;
that ordinary, deluded beings constantly dwell in the relishing of craving and so forth clarifies that attachment is ignorance.

Furthermore, the Buddha renounced [the world] and, exalting the noble while rebuking the ordinary, he criticized the foolish commoners for their attachment to flavors, distinguishing the ordinary from the noble.
He taught that "this body is not firm, like a reed," and so forth, contemplating the body as empty.
Looking downward at impermanence, one first correctly contemplates it: "Who among the wise... and so forth; this section below uses the perspective of the Sages to manifest faults.
Within the preceding [section], there is a general discussion of three types of impermanence:
first, the impermanence of fragmentation, which refers to the karmic retributions of the six realms and their differentiation across the three periods of time.
Second is impermanence as the passing away of every thought-moment;
third is impermanence as the lack of substantial reality in intrinsic nature, wherein all phenomena are merely empty aggregations and possess no inherent nature whatsoever.

Now, to briefly discuss two points: first, that "this body is impermanent, not abiding for even a single thought-moment," which is the mindfulness of impermanence; and second, using metaphors such as "like a flash of lightning" to illustrate it.
The passage beginning with "This body is fragile" concerns the impermanence of the segmented (khaṇḍa) nature of existence.
The section beginning with "This body is easily destroyed, like the bank of a river" contemplates how birth is easily followed by death; it first presents the principle and then provides the analogy.
From "not for long" onwards, one contemplates that death is easily imminent.
The preceding section constitutes the formal contemplation.
The phrase "What wise person would delight in this body? cites the fact that even the noble ones do not find joy in it, thereby clarifying that the body is to be reviled.
The above constitutes the first section, the contemplation of the five faults of the body. Below this follows the second section, which reveals the loss through two matters.
These two points are explained as follows:

first, the distinction between the difficult and the easy. To "fill the ocean with the hoofprint of a cow" or to "roll the earth into a date-sized ball," even down to the size of a mote of dust—such things are extremely difficult, yet they can still be accomplished. However, to fully describe the faults of the body is ultimately impossible.

Second, the analysis of quantity: the great ocean is deep and vast, yet its volume could be exhausted by filling it with the water from a cow’s footprint; the great earth is wide and expansive, yet its mass could be exhausted by rolling it into pellets the size of jujube fruits or even dust motes. However, the afflictions of the body are more numerous than those; they cannot be fully described.
"Therefore, one should abandon it, like discarding mucus or spittle"—this is the third section, summarizing the arising of revulsion.
Thus far, the first [section] has been the contemplation of faults to give rise to revulsion.
"By these causes and conditions," and so forth, refers to the cultivation for the purpose of severing [defilements].
Because one contemplates the body as having many faults due to these causes and conditions, one cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and other [meditations] as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
The [meditations on] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are explained extensively in a separate chapter.

Regarding the fourth section, which extensively protects those of small capacity, it praises their present and future merits but does not praise their past merits; the meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
In the present section, his self-benefit and benefit for others are praised.
The text is divided into three pairs:
the first pair concerns the beginning of practice, the second the middle of practice, and the third the end of practice.
"Deeply delighting in inquiry and reception" marks the beginning of one's own practice;
"having heard it, expounding it" marks the beginning of benefiting others.
This constitutes the first pair.
"Protecting the Original Vow" and so forth constitute the sequence of self-cultivation.
One protects and upholds the original vow, guarding the bodhicitta.
From "Reviling Women" onwards is the undertaking of bodhisattva practice: first, one develops revulsion for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); next, one aspires toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), "reviling women" and so forth represent the present faults that can be loathed;
"destroying birth" and so forth represent the future faults that can be extinguished; and "thirsting with longing for the Mahāyāna" is the way to approach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The section beginning with "Having already fulfilled oneself" concerns the sequence of benefiting others;
this is the second pair.

The section beginning with "Deeply delighting in the Great [Vehicle]" marks the conclusion of one's own practice. "Deeply delighting" and "protecting" are praises of virtue from the perspective of ultimate reality: "deeply delighting" refers to the practice of gathering the Dharma, while "protecting" refers to the practice of safeguarding the Dharma.
The section beginning with "Although she manifests as a woman" clears away the provisional to reveal the real.
The section beginning with "She is well able to conform" marks the culmination of benefiting others; it refers to skillfully conforming to the world and transforming it through worldly dharmas.

The [sections on] "those who have crossed over" and "those who have not yet crossed over," etc., constitute the transformation through the teachings of the Hīnayāna, which causes them to cross over the fruit of suffering and understand its causal accumulation.
The section beginning with "Succeeding the Three Jewels" constitutes the transformation through the teachings of the Mahāyāna; this is the third pair.

In praising his future activities, it is said that he will turn toward benefiting others; by means of "great adornment" (*mahā-vyūha*) and so forth, his self-benefit is praised. This "great adornment" comprises the practice of wholesome deeds, while "firmly maintaining the prohibitions" constitutes the avoidance of unwholesome deeds.
The preceding section constitutes the specific praise;

the following summarizes it: "All have fully accomplished" and so forth concludes the previous discussion on self-benefit, while "toward all beings" and so forth concludes the aforementioned benefit for others.
The preceding section constitutes the first part, which enumerates the assembly and extols their virtues; the latter three parts may be understood accordingly.

Above, the assembly of practitioners was clarified; below, the regular followers are listed. First, the Licchavis are enumerated because they provided the most offerings, whereas those before them did so less and those after them even less; therefore, they are listed next.
The text is divided into four sections:

first, listing the assembly and praising their virtues; second, describing their service to the Buddha; third, the Tathāgata’s refusal; and fourth, the Buddha’s power causing them to abide in the air.
Within the first section, there are three parts: first, listing the assembly; second, praising their virtues; and third, listing their names.
In the initial listing of the assembly, "four Ganges" indicates the number, while "Licchavi" identifies the group.
"Licchavi" is a Sanskrit term; according to one tradition, it means "mutual governance.
They belong to this royal lineage, and because they govern state affairs through mutual consultation, they are called "Mutual Governance" (Licchavi).
The kings listed below exceed five *gaṅgā* [of worlds], and their queens exceed seven *gaṅgā*; thus, the royal lineage should be numerous. Why, then, is there only four *gaṅgā* here?
Those for whom there is a causal connection come; those for whom there is no connection do not assemble. How can the number be fixed?
Next, his virtues are praised, first by way of detailed exposition and then by way of a summary.
Within the exposition, there are three parts:

first, the practice of protecting the Dharma; second, from "May I... onwards, the clarification of the vow to protect the Dharma; and third, from "Always desiring and delighting... onwards, the clarification of the mind that protects the Dharma. Within these three sections, all benefit both oneself and others.

Within the practice of protecting the Dharma, "skillfully cultivating the precepts for the sake of seeking the Dharma" and so forth constitute the practice of gathering the Dharma; this is self-benefit.
"Subduing adversaries" and so forth constitute the practice of protecting the Dharma; this is benefit for others.
"Subduing heterodox teachers and those who destroy the True Dharma" refers to the subduing of deviant practices.

Whether they be heterodox teachers, non-Buddhists, or those with false views and no faith; or those who harbor the inner study of the True Dharma yet violate the precepts and lack proper conduct—all such individuals are subdued by means of royal power.
The section beginning with "Constantly addressing one another" refers to the general correct practice.

Constantly addressing one another means that they encourage each other to propagate the Dharma; they should use gold and other wealth to relinquish material goods in order to open the Way, providing for others so that they may study, thereby ensuring that the nectar of immortality remains long in the world.
The Buddha-dharma can eliminate the parching thirst of afflictions; thus, it is like nectar (*amṛta*).
Vast and difficult to exhaust, it is called the "Inexhaustible Dharma";
moistening and profound beyond measure, it is called the "Profound Treasury."
Within the vows for protecting the Dharma, "May I always study" constitutes the vow to embrace the Dharma, which is self-benefit;
from "slandering" onwards constitutes the vow to protect the Dharma, which is the benefit of others.
Within these four propositions, the first two punish evil and the latter two reward goodness.
Regarding the punishment of evil in the former pair: if there are those who slander the teachings or non-Buddhists who disparage the orthodoxy, their tongues shall be cut off to silence them;
if those within our own school, such as monastics, violate the precepts, they shall be expelled from the pure assembly.

In the section on rewarding goodness at the bottom, the passage beginning with “those who are able to delight” refers to those in secular life who possess faith and serve with reverence as if honoring a superior.
