The section beginning with “if there are monks” refers to those who have left the household life and possess practice; because they take joy in providing assistance like kinsmen, they are enabled to attain power.
Within the mind that protects the Dharma, “always desiring to hear” and so forth constitutes the mind that gathers the Dharma, which is self-benefit;
“also explaining it for others” constitutes the mind that communicates the Dharma, which is benefit for others.
The preceding section has been a detailed eulogy; the following section provides a summary.
The enumeration of names makes [the meaning] clear; this concludes the first section.
The subsequent two [sections] are easily understood.
In the fourth section, first it is shown that the Licchavis failed to achieve their aim and were overcome by grief; subsequently, through the power of the Buddha, they were made to abide in the void.

Why was this so? Because the Licchavis were single-mindedly devoted to protecting the Dharma, and since their merit in protecting the Dharma was supreme, the Buddha caused them to abide in the void so as to provide a model for others to emulate.

Regarding "seven *tāla*": one *tāla* tree is seven *ren* above the ground; one *ren* is seven feet. Thus, one tree is forty-nine feet in total, and seven trees are three hundred and forty-three feet in total.

Next are listed the great ministers and various elders; they are also placed after [the laymen] because their offerings were more numerous at the front and fewer at the rear. This section also has four parts: first, listing the assembly and praising their virtues;

second, explaining the assembly’s praise of virtues; third, listing their names, which can be understood from the text; and fourth... [etc.]。 The listing of the assembly and the praise of their virtues may be understood from the text.
Second, regarding the two offerings made to the Buddha, which are five times the former, one should look back to the first five mentioned;
third, the Tathāgata did not accept them;
fourth, the Buddha’s power caused him to abide in the air, and because this was also for the sake of protecting the Dharma, he remained suspended in the air.
Next, the various kings are listed; because their human offerings were more numerous at the beginning and fewer toward the end, they are placed here.

The text is divided into six sections: first, listing their retinues; second, explaining the offering articles; third, praising their virtues; fourth, presenting the offerings to the Buddha; fifth, the Tathāgata’s non-acceptance; and sixth, failing to succeed and remaining behind.
Within the first section, that which has been collected is first clarified.
The phrase "excluding Ajātaśatru" and following serves to distinguish those who have not been included.
Because one who kills his father in this world feels such profound shame and dread, he does not appear here.
Their names are listed below; for what reason are their numbers not enumerated?
It is because the kings exceed five *gaṅgā* [rivers] but do not yet reach six *gaṅgā*s, and since their boundaries cannot be clearly defined, they are omitted and not listed.
The second [section] is clear.
In the third section, which offers praise, there is first the self and then others.

Within the four phrases concerning the self, the first two phrases describe abandoning the heterodox to return to the orthodox, while the latter two phrases describe discarding the minor to embrace the great.
The benefit to others can be understood; the latter three are easy to explain.
Next, the ladies-in-waiting are listed; this is because offerings from common people were more numerous at the beginning and fewer toward the end, hence they are listed here.
There are four distinct sections in the text:
First, the assembly ranks and praises his virtues; second, they offer service to the Buddha; third, the Tathāgata does not accept it; fourth, failing to achieve their aim, they stand back.
Within the first [section], there are four parts: first, ranking the assembly; second, praising their virtues; third, listing their names; and fourth, further praising their virtues.

In the initial listing of the assembly, "the seven *ganges* of ladies" correctly enumerates those who have gathered; the phrase "excluding *Ajātaśatru*" and those following it distinguishes those who have not yet assembled.
Since King Śreṇya has not yet arrived, the same applies to his ladies: they follow the king and have not yet come.

In the second section of the praise, "for the sake of delivering those currently appearing as women" refers to the virtue of benefiting others, while "constantly contemplating the body and so forth" refers to the virtue of self-benefit; these may be understood by listing their names.

In the fourth section on praise, the first part clarifies self-benefit: "abiding securely" encompasses the cultivation of goodness, while "practicing the precepts" prevents evil; "compassion for the lowly" clarifies benefiting others; the final three points may be understood accordingly.
Next, the celestial maidens are enumerated; the text is divided into six sections: first, the enumeration of their host;

second, the detailed description of their offerings beginning with "They spoke these words"; third, the praise of their virtues; fourth, the explanation of their service to the Buddha; fifth, the Tathāgata’s refusal; and sixth, their failure to succeed and remaining at a distance.
The first section may be understood as it stands.
In the second section, the initial part consists of mutual exhortation; one observes what others have prepared, and from the words "We too," onwards, one intends to offer it oneself.
Within this, there are four points:
first, the acceptance of offerings;
second, the recollection that the Buddha, having accepted them, shall enter nirvana, which demonstrates the necessity of performing these acts.
The final offering to the Buddha among the Three Clarities is extremely difficult to achieve; this demonstrates that it must be performed.
Fourth, by citing the emptiness of the world after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it clarifies that one should now make offerings.
Within the third section on praise, there is first a specific exposition and subsequently a conclusion.
Within the section on "Distinction," its merits of the present and future are praised, while those of the past are not; the meaning is the same as explained previously.
Within the section on the "Present," its self-benefit and benefit for others are praised.
The text contains three pairs:
The first pair concerns the beginning of practice; the second, the middle of practice; and the third, the end of practice.
"Delighting in and wishing to hear" is the beginning of self-benefit;
"having heard it, [teaching] for others" is the beginning of benefiting others—this constitutes the first pair.
"Thirsting for and aspiring to the Mahāyāna" refers to the sequence of self-benefit;
"having already fulfilled oneself" and below refers to the sequence of benefiting others—this constitutes the second pair.

"Guarding the Great [Vehicle]" and so forth mark the conclusion of self-benefit; therein, the practice of gathering wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgraha*) is first clarified, wherein the protection of the Dharma serves as that gathering of wholesome qualities.
"Guarding the great" is the general [principle], while the section beginning with "if there is anything different" specifically reveals the characteristics of protection.
Being fully equipped with the observance of precepts is the practice of avoiding transgressions;

the section beginning with "skillfully following" represents the culmination of benefiting others. "Skillfully following the world" refers to the transformation through worldly dharmas, while "delivering those not yet delivered" and so forth refer to the transformation through supramundane dharmas; this constitutes the third pair.
The subsequent praise of the future—“he shall turn the Dharma,” and so forth—refers to his benefit for others; “with great adornment,” and so forth, refers to his self-benefit.
Thus far has been the individual praise.

The following summarizes this: "Accomplishing such virtues" concludes the preceding section on self-benefit; "bestowing equal compassion upon living beings" and below conclude the aforementioned benefit for others.
Within the fourth section, which discusses making offerings to the Buddha, there are four distinct parts:

first, a detailed exposition of the articles of offering. There are ten such articles, namely: incense, wood, canopies, curtains, banners, sweet delicacies, music, couches and seats, lamps, and flowers.
Second, he contemplated that the Buddha was about to pass away, and his heart was filled with sorrow and distress;
third, he went to the Buddha for the sake of rebirth, as explained previously;
fourth, he requested the Buddha to accept his offerings.
The latter two [sections] may be understood.

Among the assemblies such as the nāgas, the sequence is generally as follows: first, the assembly is enumerated; next, their offerings to the Buddha are explained; and finally, from the passage "The Tathāgata did not accept them" onwards, they fail to achieve their aim and withdraw. This textual structure is clear and may be understood accordingly.

Up to this point, the numbers have been listed in gradual increments, whereas from "twenty great fragrant elephants as numerous as the Ganges" onwards, the various assemblies are listed in a disordered sequence.
As for the phrase "At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs of Jambudvīpa, all gathered together," how does this differ from what was stated above, such that it is listed again?

The former assembly consisted solely of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whereas this one encompasses both the higher and lower stages; since both ordinary beings and noble ones have gathered here, it is called "all," with the sole exception of the retinues of Kāśyapa and Ānanda.
Ānanda was being harassed by Māra outside the Ārāma, and for this reason he has not yet arrived.
Kāśyapa arrived later, and the Buddha manifested his two feet to bring great benefit to many people; for this reason, they have not yet assembled.
Question: When the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, Gavāmpati was in the heavens and did not come; why was he not excluded?
The explanation says:
Kāśyapa and Ānanda, though they have not yet arrived, will certainly come in the future; for this reason, they are excluded here.
Kuvana, however, remains in heaven and will ultimately never come; therefore, he is not excluded at this time.
Examples of this kind are surely not limited to one; this concludes the fifth section.
From here on follows the sixth: the Tathāgata transforms the forest to consolidate the minds of the assembly.
Why was this necessary?

When the new assembly had arrived and saw that the Buddha was still present, they hoped the Sage would not pass away, and their feelings of attachment remained lingering; therefore, the Buddha transformed the grove to manifest his passing, thereby earnestly exhorting them.
In this passage, there is first an analysis, followed by an analogy, and finally a synthesis.
Within the analysis, it is first stated that the forest is transformed into white; because this clarifies its brilliant whiteness, it is said to be "like a crane."
Why does it appear white?
People say that the color white is a sign of a tree’s death, intended to symbolize the passing away of the Sage.
This has already been refuted above.
Furthermore, another person says:
"White is the fundamental nature of form.
This reveals that the Buddha returns to the source.
While this may perhaps be so, it is not what is taught in the sūtras and thus cannot be definitively established.

Next, as for the manifestation of the Jewel Hall that illuminates the Twin Śāla Trees, people have likewise proposed various differing interpretations; since these are difficult to discern, let us cease for now.
Below, springs and pools appear, filled with exquisite flowers that adorn and embellish the jeweled hall; the correspondence between these elements can be understood through analogy.

Based on this textual alignment, it is certain that the grove and the hall do not constitute separate entities. Only after the appearance of the hall is the grove described, with its various adornments and its extreme beauty.
From here on, the seventh section further clarifies how the assembled multitudes, upon beholding the signs, increase their compassion and present offerings.
This section contains two parts:
first, it clarifies how the multitudes gathered in this location, upon beholding the signs, increase their compassion and present offerings.
Second: From "At that time, to the east of here" onwards, it clarifies the gathering of multitudes from other directions to present offerings.

Within the first section, it first clarifies the perception of signs; that all were moved by grief is an intensification of compassion, which is termed the transformation of the forest into the sign of *nirvāṇa*. Below, it clarifies the presentation of offerings.
Question: Are these the same as the previous assembly?
Explanation:
The *kāma-devas* and *asuras* are subsumed within the two aforementioned groups of devas and asuras; they are mentioned here once again.
Therefore, although the Four Kings were listed in the preceding text, they are raised again now, and the same applies to the others.
The newly arrived assembly of Brahmās is as listed below.
Since the gods of the desire realm and the asuras are already part of the preceding assembly, why is it that offerings are discussed only now?
The explanation is as follows:

These [beings] previously came from the void; having reached the Twin Trees and seeing the various preparations, they only then conceived the intention to make offerings. Therefore, they are listed here, and thus it is said below: "Observe how humans and devas have made great offerings; we, too, shall offer."

Furthermore, it may be that both the people and the offerings arrive together; if the number of people increases while the offerings gradually increase, listing them as before would be appropriate. However, if there are many people but few offerings, or conversely, if there are few people but many offerings, listing them as before would be inconvenient; therefore, this is explained here.

Within this, there are six sections: first, the offering presented by the gods of the desire realm’s terrestrial heavens; second, the offering presented by the gods of the desire realm’s celestial space; third, the offerings presented by the various Brahmās; fourth, the offering presented by the asura Vemacitra; fifth, the offering presented by the Māra kings; and sixth, the offering presented by the Great Lord Maheśvara. These are arranged here according to the progressive increase in their respective offerings.
The first section has three parts:
first, the detailed discussion and offering presented by the Four Kings and Śakra; second, the offerings presented by the Four Kings; third, the offerings presented by Śakra.
Regarding the first part, the passage beginning with "You all observe the devas and humans" concerns the observation of what others have established.
The passage beginning with "We also" expresses their own desire to offer [the gift].
The passage beginning with "If I am the most... cites the signs of benefit through contemplation.

Within the offerings presented by the Four Kings, the primary donors are first identified: on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, there are four *Nandana* mountains, situated forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth, and equal in length and breadth.
Above are the Four Kings:

the Heavenly King of the East is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó); he leads the various celestial hosts along with the two classes of ghosts and spirits, the Gandharvas and the Piśācas.

The Heavenly King of the South is named Virūḍhaka, which means "Lord of Increase" (Zēngzhǎngzhǔ); he leads the various celestial hosts along with the two classes of ghosts and spirits, the Kumbhāṇḍas and the Pretas.
The Heavenly King of the West is named Virūpākṣa, which translates as "Varied Speech"; he leads the various celestial hosts as well as the two classes of spirits, the nāgas and the piśācas.
The Heavenly King of the North is named Vaiśravaṇa, which translates as "Much Hearing"; he leads the various celestial hosts as well as the two classes of spirits, the yakṣas and the rākṣasas.
Therefore, Vaisravana was previously listed among the ghost kings; these Four Great Kings have now come to present their offerings.
From the phrase "that which is prepared" onwards, the text explains the offerings made to the Buddha.
"Twice as much as before" means twice as much as all that had been prepared above.
When the Buddha set it down, he did not accept it; failing to achieve his purpose, [Indra] withdrew and stood back.

Among the offerings presented by Śakra, the host of the offering is first identified: Śakra-devānām-indra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which in this translation is named "The One Able to Act as King of the Gods."

The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) is presented here along with its hosts; atop Mount Sumeru there are thirty-three distinct locations, with Śakra residing in the center. Each side has eight nations where the subjects and citizens dwell; therefore, it is collectively called the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Next, the offering is explained: it was doubled beyond the previous amount, doubled beyond that of the Four Kings, and could even be doubled beyond all that had been previously prepared.
The Tathāgata did not accept it, and the result was the same as before.

Down to the sixth section, "That Which Is Provided" and below, this refers to the offerings presented by the empty deities of the desire realm; beginning from Yāma Heaven up to Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, all come to present these offerings, the textual details of which may be understood accordingly.
Among the various offerings presented by the Brahmās, there are five distinct sections.
First, a general clarification that the entire assembly of Brahmās has gathered, extending upward as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

As for those who have "all come," this refers to reaching the Peak of Existence within the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*); those in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not mentioned because they lack physical form.
It may also extend upward to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception.
As for those in the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-dhyāna), how do they come?
To explain:
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not see them, and thus they are said to be "formless"; yet they exist in reality, and therefore it can be said that they come.
Thus, it is stated in the *Āgama*: "When Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, the devas of the formless realms all came to shed tears, like a fine spring rain."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also states: "The olfactory faculty of a bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm.
Since this same scripture further explains that there are forms [in those realms], beings from up to the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) all come forth.
Because those above the realm of form have all transcended desire, they are collectively termed the "Assembly of Brahmā" (Brahmaparṣad).
Second, from the words "At that time" onwards, the specific patrons of the offerings are designated.
Since among those previously gathered there were both those who provided offerings and those who did not, they are mentioned separately here.
This must be the Brahmā King of the Intermediate Heaven.
How is this known? Since the shorter banner hangs only from the Brahma palace, it is clearly understood that it is not from above.
This may also refer to the Brahma King of the Third Dhyāna;
third, the Buddha was served by the Three Eloquences;
fourth, the Tathāgata did not accept [the offering].
The fifth is "not succeeding and remaining behind.

In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the leader is first designated; since this is a great bodhisattva, he emits bodily radiance that surpasses that of Brahmā, covering a thousand worlds. Regarding his refusal of the offerings, it is the same as before.
Within the offering by the Māra King, there are six distinct sections:
first, identifying the donor and praising his deed; second, explaining the presentation of offerings to the Buddha; [and so forth].
Third, the divine incantation for the three offerings;
fourth, the invitation for the Buddha to accept the offerings;
fifth, the Buddha’s consent to receive the incantation but his refusal to accept the offerings.
Sixth, "not turning back and remaining.

Regarding the beginning, "Māra Pāpīyān of the Desire Realm" identifies the host of offerings; *māra* is a Sanskrit term, which here means "the slayer," because he harms the goodness of sentient beings.

Pāpīyān is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "extremely evil. Having obtained wholesome benefits by relying on the Buddha-dharma, he does not think of repaying them, but instead wishes to inflict harm; therefore, he is named "Extremely Evil."

Within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), there is a separate realm of Māra; since this is also subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, it is now referred to as the Māra King of the Desire Realm. Many Bodhisattvas manifest themselves here through their transformative power, and thus they lead their retinues to come here to make offerings.
"Opening the Hells" below praises his deeds: first he rescues those from the sufferings of hell, and subsequently he gathers the subjects of Māra.
Within the section on rescuing from the sufferings of hell, the first part clarifies what is bestowed upon them, and the latter part clarifies what they are led away from.
What is it that is given?
It is the giving of happiness and the giving of goodness. Opening the prison and providing water is the giving of happiness;
from the words "thereupon he informed" onwards is the giving of goodness.
Building upon the previous act of offering water, he further exhorted him toward goodness; thus it is called "thereby informing.
"You are incapable" indicates what he is unable to endure—that is, his inability to provide for the Buddha.

From "Only you should" onwards, [the text] gauges their capacity and instructs them to cultivate wholesome thoughts; it first teaches mindfulness of the Buddha and subsequently teaches sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

From "You should cause" onwards, it clarifies the benefits of cultivation: the slumber of birth and death is called "night," the boundless cycle of transmigration is called "long," and attaining the goodness of self-serenity is termed "gaining peace"; this explains what is bestowed.

The passage beginning with "Māra completely removes the blades from hell" clarifies what he says: [he claims] to remove swords and rain down water to extinguish fires. However, these are the karmic retributions of sentient beings; how could Māra possibly dispel them?
It cannot be attained directly; rather, through the exhortations of previous teachings, by recollecting the Buddha and rejoicing in merit, the defilements of sin are thinned and thus eliminated.

Furthermore, Māra is actually an inconceivable Bodhisattva; those who encounter him must surely have been virtuous people in past lives whose karmic retributions can be transformed, and it is for this reason that he acts to remove their obstacles.

Just as when a person is impoverished, although it is the result of past karma, they can be rescued with wealth; so it is with him: he rescues those in the suffering of hell above and gathers the subjects of Māra below. By means of the Buddha’s spiritual power, he gives rise to this intention, and having again brought forth this mind, he once more arouses the will to transform others.

The passage beginning with "Command all those... and below admonishes the relinquishing of weapons of combat. Since Māra specializes in causing disruption and confusion, he frequently uses weapons of combat to terrify practitioners when they are destroying their own roots of goodness; this section now exhorts them to abandon such things.

The second section, the explanation of the offerings, is clear in its text and may be understood accordingly. Within the third section, the recitation of the mantra for presentation, there are six distinct parts:
first, the self-proclamation of one’s own mind, manifesting one’s love for the Dharma;
second, from the words "Men and women, as an offering," onwards, it clarifies the purpose of the mantra, which is for the sake of all those who uphold the Dharma.
3. From "Truṭi" onwards, the mantra text itself is proclaimed;
4. From "This mantra can" onwards, the efficacy of the mantra is explained;
5. From "In order to subdue" onwards, the intent of the mantra's recitation is clarified.
Sixth: The section beginning with "If there are those who can" clarifies the benefits obtained by those who uphold [the Dharma]; it may also be termed "Exhortation to Uphold by Highlighting Benefits.
Within this, the initial part—"We love and delight in the Mahāyāna"—is the mind that embraces the Dharma;
"protecting the Mahāyāna" is the mind that guards the Dharma.
Māra is largely deceitful; fearing that the Buddha would not believe him, he uttered these words to manifest his own sincerity.
In the second section, it is clarified that he has already recited this mantra as a protection for those who receive the Dharma, in order to prevent [obstacles].

Human beings encompass both the true and the false: acting for the sake of the Way and for the sake of others is termed "true," while acting for the sake of the body and for the sake of wealth is described as "false.
Within this text, there is a detailed discussion that should be divided into three parts:
First, its authenticity is presented; second, its falsity is distinguished; third, from "or authentic or false" onwards, both authenticity and falsity are cited together.
Having already explained this for the sake of clarification, the text contains only two [sections], as the presentation of authenticity is omitted for brevity.
The false still act, whereas the true remains beyond words; therefore, I shall briefly omit them.
Within the category of the false, there are five types:
"Practicing for the sake of making offerings" refers to upholding the sutras and the Dharma in order to obtain the four requisites of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine.
"Out of fear" means fearing the various sufferings of the present and the evil realms of the future;
"to deceive others" means to mislead others so that they will hold oneself in respect;
"for the sake of wealth and profit" means for the purpose of obtaining gold, silver, treasuries, and other such things.
"To act for the sake of others" means to yield to the pressure of others while lacking sincerity oneself.
Because of these five matters, one accepts this Mahāyāna; therefore, it is called "false."
Generally speaking, what is received from all the sūtras and dharmas is entirely spurious.
Now, in contrast to this sūtra, we speak of receiving the "Great" [Vehicle]; yet the spurious is immeasurable, and for now we cite only these five.
Among these five, fear pertains exclusively to the body;
offerings and material gain pertain exclusively to wealth;
deceiving others and following others pertain to both body and wealth.

I shall set forth the subject matter: whether it be a true document concerning what was previously omitted, or a false document concerning what has been debated as spurious—for such people, I shall eliminate their fear by reciting this mantra; this is stated in general terms.
The beneficial matters are not limited to one; the power of its function in removing fear is particularly strong, which is why it is singled out for mention.
This is the third incantation.
For what reason is it not translated?
If translated or altered, their efficacy would be lost and they would frequently fail to produce spiritual results; this is why they were not translated.

Furthermore, the words of these dhāraṇīs do not necessarily constitute the specific language of India alone; since translators did not understand them, they were not translated. This is generally the case for most dhāraṇī passages in various sūtras, which are left untranslated.

In the fourth [clause], the meaning of the words is insufficient; if it were complete, it should state that this mantra can cause those who have lost their minds, those who are terrified, those who speak [fearfully], and those who do not maintain the Dharma to be free from all terrors.
The avoidance of fear is as explained later in the section on "Benefits of Upholding," and thus it is not mentioned here.

As for the term "loss of mind" (*citta-vipraṇāśa*), it refers to the lowest among the types of hypocrisy. Among the four types of hypocrites previously mentioned—those who deceive others for the sake of offerings and those who follow others for the sake of wealth—these individuals have lost their wholesome resolve for renunciation; therefore, they are called "those who have lost their minds."
The term "fear" refers to the most excellent among the false, meaning that within the preceding category of the false, fear is supreme.
The term "preaching the Dharma" refers to the most excellent among the true, namely, the proclamation of the Mahāyāna sūtra teachings.

Regarding "the dharma of non-interruption": this refers to the inferior aspect within the truth; that is to say, those who do not sever the Small Vehicle teachings—because their provisional transformations never cease—it is called the dharma of non-interruption.
By the power of this mantra, because it universally protects all four assemblies, both great and small are included.
For these four types of people, the mantra is able to eliminate all fears.
In the fifth section, which clarifies the intent of the mantras spoken by Māra, there is first a detailed exposition followed by a summary.
Within the four-line exposition, the first two lines concern persons and the latter two concern the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of human beings," the initial statement "in order to subdue non-Buddhists" clarifies the purpose of the teaching in contrast to those previously mentioned who do not sever the dharmas; it is for the sake of enabling such persons to propagate the True Dharma and to defeat non-Buddhists that this mantra is taught to protect them.

Regarding "protecting one's own person": for those who have previously lost their minds or are filled with fear, this is explained to clarify what is to be done; so that such persons may obtain this divine mantra to protect themselves and uphold the sutra and its Dharma, the mantra is thus recited for them.

Regarding those who protect the True Dharma within the teachings: those who protect the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Māra intends to protect the Śrāvaka vehicle and thus recites mantras to protect those who do not sever the preceding dharmas;
those who protect the Mahāyāna, the Māra intends to protect the Mahāyāna and thus recites mantras to protect those who previously expounded the Great Dharma.
"Recite this mantra" serves as the general conclusion.
Regarding the sixth holder, among the benefits obtained, one first attains the benefit of the Dharma; this is evident from the text, which first enumerates and subsequently concludes [the section].

"Those who uphold this mantra, we shall protect"—the following section describes the benefits obtained by such a person. "We protect those who uphold it" means that, like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs, we protect them from the loss of their former resolve and from fear, ensuring they suffer no decline or affliction; the tortoise withdraws its four legs, with its head and tail making six.

I am not being flatterous; rather, with utmost sincerity and increased effort, I assist those who have spoken as before and those who do not sever the Dharma, so as to augment their power of exposition. Desiring that those who transmit the Dharma in the future may recognize that Māra truly protects [the Dharma] and thus resolve to propagate it, I speak of "sincerity" and "augmenting with utmost truth."
The preceding six sections together constitute the third part, the "Mantra for Offering to the Deities.
The fourth part, "Inviting the Buddha to Accept the Offerings," is as can be understood.

Within the fifth section, first there is the non-acceptance of offerings, next the acceptance of the mantra, and finally the clarification of the intent behind accepting [the mantra], which is to bring peace to the fourfold assembly.
Based on this, it is certain that Māra’s intention applies universally to all upholders of the Dharma, not merely to those of this specific sutra.
Below, [the Buddha] remains silent and does not accept [the challenge]. The sixth [section], where he fails to achieve his goal and withdraws as before, is the same as the preceding case.
Within the context of Maheśvara, the primary patron of the offering is first identified.
Maheśvara is none other than the celestial king Mahesvara; as Nāgārjuna stated:
"Above the Five Pure Abodes, there is a distinct realm of Bodhisattva Pure Abodes called Maheśvara, wherein Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are mostly reborn."
"Now I have come to present this offering.
From the words "that which has been prepared" below, the text explains the honoring and offering to the Buddha; herein there are three parts:
first, explaining that the offerings were made prior to [the arrival] and carried to the Buddha's location.
2. From "Having addressed the Buddha" onwards, it demonstrates that although the offering was modest, the field of merit—the Buddha—is weighty;
3. From "Therefore" onwards, he requests that the Buddha compassionately accept [the offering].
The first section is clear.
Within the second section, there are three distinct parts:

first, manifesting that the offering was already minute; second, from "If one were to take a trichiliocosm... onwards, using the many to illustrate the few; and third, from "Why? onwards, providing the explanation.
In the preceding section, first is the teaching (dharma), next is the illustration (upamā), and finally is the application (anusandhi).
The explanation of the teaching is clear.
Within the illustrations, five distinct metaphors are first presented individually.
Regarding the first analogy, the mosquito represents oneself and the "I" represents the Tathāgata; the remaining four [elements] can be understood accordingly.
From the phrase "How could there be... onwards, it concludes that what was previously described as minute and insignificant is incapable of benefiting the many.
What is "few"? That which is offered by those with sovereign power.
What is "many"? [That which is offered by others.]
This refers to the fruit of reliance (āśraya-phala) of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.
Only the latter four [verses] are concluded; the first metaphor is not discussed.

"How could it benefit the great ocean? concludes the second preceding point, clarifying that a single handful of water does not benefit the great ocean, serving as a metaphor for how what one has offered does not benefit the fruit of reliance of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.
"How could it benefit the daily brightness? concludes the third point, clarifying that a single small lamp does not benefit many suns;
"How could it benefit the multitude of flowers? concludes the fourth point, clarifying that a single flower does not benefit a multitude of flowers;
"How could it benefit Mount Sumeru? concludes the fifth point, clarifying that a single pavilion does not benefit Mount Sumeru.
The lower comparison may be understood accordingly.
Above, the first section correctly expounded the subtlety of the offerings; below this, the second section cites the many to reveal the few.

Since the Buddha’s virtues and grace are profound, even if one were to fill the entire trichiliocosm with offering implements to present as worship, it would still be insufficient to describe; how much more so then our own preparations—how could they not be subtle and meager?
From this point downward is the third section, which raises the theme of the Buddha’s profound kindness to explain why the previous offerings were insufficient.
"For what reason? is the question.
For what reason is it that even the offerings of a trichiliocosm are still called insufficient?
The following provides an explanation of this.

Taking the Buddha as one’s parent, he constantly rescues those suffering in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; therefore, even making offerings of a trichiliocosm is still called insufficient.
“Hell” (dìyù) is called *niraya* in foreign lands.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* explains: “That which is supremely loathsome is named *niraya*.
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains: “Because it is not to be enjoyed, it is named hell (*naraka*).*”
The meaning is the same. These two meanings both manifest the faults [of hell] in contrast to the mind of revulsion; they do not represent its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the correct understanding of its essential characteristic, the name is established according to its location: since the subterranean prison is its place of birth, it is called "earth-hell" (*naraka*).
Regarding the term "preta" (hungry ghost), the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* explains: "They are called 'hungry ghosts' because they seek from others.
Furthermore, they are called "hungry" because they are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst;
they are called "ghosts" because they are timid and full of fear.

Regarding the term "animal" (*tiryag-yoni*), the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Zaxin) explains: "Because they move horizontally, they are called animals. This is an analysis of their characteristics, not an etymological explanation of the term's meaning.
The name "beast" (*tiryagyoni*) is derived from the primary sense of being raised for maintenance.
Because all worldly people raise these beings either for consumption as food or for labor and service, they are called "beasts" (*tiryag-yoni*) based on this partial meaning.
Regarding "the various evil realms," this refers to the asuras and others.
Because the Buddha constantly rescues sentient beings who suffer in these places, one should offer extensive offerings to him.
From the beginning up to this point constitutes the second section, which clarifies the offering already made.
From here on is the third section, requesting the Buddha’s compassionate acceptance.
Since the Buddha exists for the sake of sentient beings, constantly rescuing them from suffering in the evil realms, he should now take pity on me and accept this humble offering.
For what reason is there no Buddha here who does not accept [the offering], nor who turns back without fruition?
Some explain, saying: "Because guests from other directions have arrived, he is briefly absent.
This should not be so; even if guests were to arrive, what would prevent him from not accepting [the offering] or turning back without fruition?
This is simply because the compiler of the sutra omitted it;
it was transcribed from the Great Sutra Repository of Kanzeon-ji by the preceptor Jū on the tenth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Eikyō era.
Hōin Gendai Sōjū Kenpō (The Dharma Seal, Great Monastic Head, Kenpō)
